All adults are flightless females that reproduce parthenogenetically. The absence of wings and the distinct head shape distinguish it from other citrus weevils like the cribrate weevil.

Q1:
<image>
This orange has small black spots scattered on the peel—some tiny, some a bit bigger, and a few with faint reddish edges. Is this likely black spot disease?
Q2: Does this orange exhibit small black spots of varying sizes on its peel, some with faint reddish margins?
label: Yes, this matches early-stage Alternaria black spot (caused by Alternaria alternata). The key visual evidence is the scattered dark brown to black spots of varying sizes on mature yellow-orange fruit, some with subtle reddish-brown halos—consistent with initial fruit infection before lesions become deeply sunken or develop visible black specks (conidiomata). Septoria spot typically shows more uniformly sunken, larger black lesions with distinct fruiting bodies and often appears after color break; here, spots are mostly superficial and lack pronounced depression or embedded black dots, making Alternaria more probable.

Q1:
<image>
The leaf edges are yellow with a dark green center, but there are no holes or insects present—what could be the issue?
Q2: What is causing the yellowing along the leaf margins while the center remains dark green, with no signs of insect damage or holes?
label: One of the early typical symptoms of Huanglongbing (HLB) is mottled yellowing, caused by bacterial blockage in the phloem that disrupts nutrient transport. The key diagnostic feature is the irregular, asymmetric distribution of yellowing across the midrib, with no signs of mechanical injury or pest damage. Recommended on-site verification: inspect the leaf undersides for the absence of psyllid nymphs or honeydew, then compare young and old leaves on the same branch—persistent yellowing in new shoots strongly indicates systemic infection rather than nutrient deficiency.

Q1:
<image>
Only one or two leaves have holes, while the rest look fine—should I spray pesticides across the entire garden?
Q2: Are pesticides necessary for the whole garden when only one or two leaves show holes and all others appear unaffected?
label: Full-orchard spraying is not currently necessary. Instead, implement targeted local intervention: remove severely damaged new shoots (including old leaves with eggs), and destroy them centrally. Spray 77% copper hydroxide (600-fold dilution) or 25% bromothalonil (800-fold dilution) within a radius of 3–5 trees surrounding the affected branches to protect new growth. Simultaneously set up yellow sticky traps to monitor adult insect density. If, within the next 7 days, ≥3 new leaves show signs of damage, escalate to full-orchard management. Based on the grading criteria, this already meets Level 1 threshold (2–3 adults per plant with visible notching). confidence: 0.91

Q1:
<image>
The leaves are curled extremely tightly, with a bulging center—could they possibly have been chewed from inside by some tiny insect?
Q2: Are the tightly curled leaves with a bulging center indicative of internal feeding by a small insect?
label: This is not caused by chewing damage but by passive leaf curling induced by dense feeding of sucking pests (like the apple yellow aphid) on the leaf’s inner surface. Aphid saliva contains plant hormone analogs that stimulate uneven cell growth at the leaf margins, resulting in inward curling that forms a protective shelter. The absence of feeding traces (notches, holes), frass, or silk webbing rules out damage by lepidopteran larvae. The bulging areas are actually internal cavities formed by curling, often harboring dozens of aphids—verification requires careful unfolding of the leaf.

Q1:
<image>
If this insect lands on a new shoot of an apple tree, how will the leaves change?
Q2: What leaf changes occur when this insect settles on a young apple tree shoot?
label: If the winged aphid successfully lays eggs or gives birth and establishes itself, its offspring (wingless nymphs) will densely attach to the undersides of new shoot leaves and feed on sap, resulting in leaves folding longitudinally along the midrib, becoming brittle, and changing color from green to pale yellow or mottled yellow-green. When leaf curling exceeds 10%, the economic threshold is reached, impairing photosynthetic efficiency and potentially triggering sooty mold disease. Note: early-stage curling typically appears only as slight tip curling—carefully examine the leaf underside for dense colonies of small insects and honeydew.

Q1:
<image>
Some leaves are curling—could this be due to insect damage or is it a sign of plant disease?
Q2: Is leaf curling in the image caused by insect activity or a plant disease?
label: Leaf rolling is a secondary symptom: after gray weevils cause marginal damage, the loss of structural balance induces local distortion and curling of the leaf. Additionally, adult females puncture the petiole base when laying eggs, which can also trigger rolling. If leaf rolling occurs alongside notching and is confined to the middle-to-lower branches, it is highly likely due to insect damage. To confirm, carefully open the base of the rolled leaf and check for tiny puncture holes or milky white larvae; this helps rule out viral diseases or mite infestations (which typically present with stippling spots or webbing).

Q1:
<image>
The leaves don’t show obvious yellow spots, but the fruit has rust-like markings—could this be caused by another type of insect?
Q2: Does the presence of rust-like markings on the fruit—without yellow spots on the leaves—indicate insect involvement?
label: It is highly likely to be citrus red mite rather than other pests. The rust-like spots are actually characteristic "silver scars" caused by accumulations of numerous molted exoskeletons, secretions, and necrotic debris—distinct from the wax powder piles of scale insects, the uniform copper-green discoloration of rust mites, or the loose black sooty mold layer of sooty mold disease. Furthermore, no scales, fungal hyphae, or galls are visible in the image; leaves show only slight curling without perforations or deformities, ruling out pests like leaf miners or diseases such as anthracnose. This symptom is most apparent during fruit color change and serves as a diagnostic indicator of citrus red mite infestation.

Q1:
<image>
Does the presence of a wrinkled, glossy, silvery-white lesion localized at the leaf tip—caused by citrus leafminer (Phyllocnistis citrella) larval mining beneath the epidermis—induce premature abscission of the entire leaf due to disruption of vascular continuity and induction of ethylene-mediated abscission zone activation?
Q2: Does the image show a wrinkled, glossy, silvery-white lesion at the leaf tip—resulting from citrus leafminer larval mining under the epidermis—that leads to premature leaf drop due to vascular disruption and ethylene-triggered abscission zone activation?
label: Yes, the presence of a wrinkled, glossy, silvery-white lesion at the leaf tip—characteristic of citrus leafminer (Phyllocnistis citrella) infestation—can trigger premature leaf drop. This lesion results from serpentine, epidermal-mining larvae that feed within the palisade mesophyll, causing mechanical separation of epidermal layers and localized accumulation of air in the mined tract, which produces the diagnostic glossy, silvery appearance. The associated epidermal collapse and distortion induce severe physiological stress, disrupt phloem transport, and provoke reactive ethylene synthesis in adjacent tissues; this upregulates cell wall–hydrolyzing enzymes (e.g., cellulase and polygalacturonase) in the leaf petiole abscission zone, accelerating cell separation and leading to premature abscission—even when only the distal portion of the leaf is visibly mined.

Q1:
<image>
Why are only certain leaves heavily notched while nearby ones look untouched?
Q2: Why do some leaves show severe notching while adjacent leaves remain unaffected?
label: Gray weevils exhibit strong preference for newly expanded, soft-textured leaves on current-season shoots; untouched leaves are either older (tougher, less palatable) or shaded/less accessible. The clustering of damage on specific branches suggests localized adult aggregation—often near previous-year oviposition sites (e.g., top two mature leaves near shoot tips). This patchiness reflects behavioral selectivity, not random feeding.

Q1:
<image>
Does the brown color with dark patches mean it’s adapted to a certain environment?
Q2: Does the brown discoloration accompanied by dark patches indicate environmental adaptation?
label: Yes—the brown base with darker mottling is crypsis for dry, bare, or senescent vegetation (e.g., stubble fields, weedy margins, or drought-stressed crops). This coloration helps avoid bird predation and is typical of grasshoppers in open, disturbed habitats. It does not indicate disease or stress; rather, it reflects normal phenotypic plasticity. If surrounding fields are green and lush, such coloration may signal the insect originated from adjacent uncultivated, dry areas—a warning that migration into crops is possible as host plants dry out.

Q1:
<image>
Some bugs look shiny black, others pale yellowish—could this be more than one pest species?
Q2: Do the shiny black and pale yellowish bugs in the image represent multiple pest species?
label: It is most likely a single aphid species with color polymorphism—specifically cotton/melon aphid (Aphis gossypii), which commonly exhibits yellow, green, and dark forms within one colony. Visual confirmation: all individuals share body shape (pear-shaped, cornicles visible on abdomen), size (~1–2 mm), and feeding posture (head embedded in plant tissue). No evidence of mites (no legs visible under magnification), thrips (no fringed wings), or scale insects (no waxy cover). Mixed coloration alone does not indicate multiple species.

Q1:
<image>
The leaf margin is yellowing, with some green still present in the center, and the veins have turned noticeably darker brown—could this be citrus greening disease (Huanglongbing)?
Q2: Does the image show yellowing leaf margins with retained central green tissue and darkened brown veins?
label: Yes, the leaf exhibits typical symptoms of citrus greening disease (HLB) with mottled chlorosis: asymmetric yellow-green mottling, chlorosis between the leaf margin and lateral veins, and significant browning and thickening of the midvein. These features closely align with phloem blockage and impaired nutrient transport caused by infection with Ca. Liberibacter asiaticus, and the absence of insect damage or mechanical injury supports the diagnosis of HLB.

Q1:
<image>
Does the presence of a California citrus swallowtail caterpillar—identified by its green body with diagonal black-and-yellow banding, prominent orange osmeterium when disturbed, and distinct black head capsule with white lateral markings—on a citrus leaf without visible feeding damage (e.g., no notching, windowing, or epidermal collapse) indicate that it is not currently causing harm to the tree?
Q2: Is a California citrus swallowtail caterpillar—characterized by a green body with diagonal black-and-yellow bands, an orange osmeterium visible when disturbed, and a black head capsule with white lateral markings—on a citrus leaf actively damaging the leaf if no feeding signs such as notching, windowing, or epidermal collapse are present?
label: The presence of a California citrus swallowtail caterpillar on a citrus leaf without observable feeding damage does not necessarily indicate absence of harm, because early-instar larvae often feed selectively on tender new growth or leaf margins in ways that may not yet manifest as macroscopic tissue loss; moreover, their feeding can induce localized physiological stress such as chlorosis or reduced photosynthetic efficiency before structural damage like notching or windowing becomes apparent. However, the absence of epidermal collapse, stippling, necrotic lesions, or frass accumulation suggests low current herbivore pressure, and the caterpillar’s developmental stage—determined by head capsule width and presence of osmeterial eversion—must be assessed to estimate potential risk: late-instar individuals exhibit exponentially higher consumption rates and are more likely to cause rapid defoliation. Therefore, visual confirmation of intact leaf lamina alone is insufficient to rule out incipient damage; monitoring for progressive marginal excision, frass deposition, and larval size progression over 24–48 hours is essential for accurate pest impact assessment.

Q1:
<image>
Only one or two leaves have holes; can we wait without spraying pesticides and see if they recover on their own?
Q2: Are the holes in just one or two leaves, and is it safe to monitor without applying pesticides?
label: Observation is not advisable. Gray weevils exhibit strong preference for tender plant tissues and a tendency to aggregate for oviposition. A single tree with 2–3 adults already reaches level 1 damage (defined as ≥2 adults per tree with visible notches). The current image shows damage on at least 3–4 leaves, indicating the outbreak has already reached the mild infestation stage. Without intervention, the population will rapidly escalate to level 2–3 (more than 4–6 adults per tree), leading to cessation of new shoot growth and decline in tree vigor. Priority should be given to non-chemical control measures: immediately manually shake off adult beetles (most effective during early morning low temperatures), and prune out old, egg-laden leaves. If more than two new notches appear within three days, chemical control must be initiated promptly to avoid missing the optimal treatment window.

Q1:
<image>
The leaves currently appear unaffected, with only two or three insects present—should I apply pesticide?
Q2: Are pesticides necessary given that the leaves show no symptoms and only two or three insects are visible?
label: Full-field pesticide application is not currently necessary, but monitoring must be intensified and preventive measures implemented: ① Use a 10x handheld magnifier to inspect the undersides of 10 new shoot leaves daily; if three or more mites per leaf are found on two consecutive days, the threshold for intervention has been reached; ② Apply a 0.5% mineral oil emulsion (e.g., Narrow Range Oil 415) to localized branches, using physical suffocation to control initial populations; ③ Avoid using broad-spectrum insecticides at this stage to prevent unintended mortality of potential natural enemies. Given that the image shows extremely low-density early-stage infestation, premature chemical control risks inducing resistance and represents unnecessary cost.

Q1:
<image>
If I scrape off this black lump, will that stop bud mites from spreading?
Q2: Does removing this black lump by scraping prevent further spread of bud mites?
label: Scraping removes only the visible residue and has no effect on citrus bud mites, which reside *inside* buds and are unaffected by surface cleaning. To manage bud mites, monitor bud infestation rates via microscopy; if needed, apply abamectin + narrow-range oil at bud swell, or release predatory mites like Neoseiulus californicus—but only after confirming live mites, as high infestation levels (>80%) often cause no economic loss.

Q1:
<image>
Its abdomen is orange, with a row of black spots along its back and legs extending from underneath its body—this doesn’t resemble a spider or an aphid; what exactly is it?
Q2: What is this insect, given its orange abdomen, a linear arrangement of black spots along its dorsal surface, and legs projecting ventrally—distinct from spiders and aphids?
label: The insect exhibits clear entomological features: distinct head, thorax, and abdomen (small head, three pairs of legs on the thorax), a hard exoskeletal structure with elytra forming a convex, oval outline dorsally, and absence of spinnerets or cerci—clearly excluding arachnids (mites) and Hemipteran aphids. The black spots are arranged in a regular, stable pattern (approximately 8–10 spots), consistent with aposematic coloration seen in certain leaf beetles (such as non-*Hippodamia convergens* ladybird-type chrysomelids) or flea beetles. It is not *Eutetranychus lewisii* (body size <0.5 mm, no distinct spots, typically found in aggregations with webbing).

Q1:
<image>
Are the brownish patches on the leaves signs of fungal disease, or part of the insect damage?
Q2: Do the brownish leaf patches indicate fungal infection or result from insect damage?
label: The brownish/grayish patches are likely secondary necrosis resulting from insect feeding—not primary fungal infection—because they occur specifically adjacent to notched margins and lack classic fungal signs (e.g., concentric rings, powdery mildew, or sporulation). In Fuller rose beetle damage, wounded tissue becomes susceptible to opportunistic pathogens like Colletotrichum or Phomopsis, leading to localized browning. However, without microscopic examination or lab testing, we cannot rule out co-infection. Visually, the spatial association with chewing damage strongly suggests insect-initiated decay. For confirmation, examine patch edges: if they follow the notch contour and lack defined margins, it supports secondary necrosis.

Q1:
<image>
The leaf surface appears slightly dark and sticky—could this be related to the presence of these insects?
Q2: Does the slight darkness and stickiness on the leaf surface correlate with the insects visible in the image?
label: It is highly likely related. Cottony cushion scale excretes large amounts of honeydew during feeding, which coats leaf surfaces and promotes the growth of sooty mold fungi, forming a gray-black fungal layer that darkens leaves and reduces reflectivity (the blurry dark spots observed in certain areas of the image support this). Honeydew itself is sticky and, upon drying, forms a thin gelatinous film. Verification method: gently wipe the leaf surface beneath the insects with a damp cloth—if black residue remains and a sweet, sticky sensation is detected, honeydew contamination is confirmed. It is advisable to simultaneously check adjacent leaf undersides for signs of spreading black sooty mold.

Q1:
<image>
Could this be citrus black spot instead of canker, since the fruit looks damaged?
Q2: Does the fruit damage in the image indicate citrus black spot rather than canker?
label: No—citrus black spot causes dark, sunken, tar-like lesions with defined margins and often a yellow halo, but never raised, cracked, polygonal corky areas. The image shows elevated, fissured, light-centered lesions typical of canker; black spot lesions remain flat or slightly depressed and do not expose underlying rind layers. Also, black spot requires prolonged leaf wetness and affects mainly mature fruit late in season, whereas canker appears on young fruit and expands rapidly under warm-wet conditions.

Q1:
<image>
If I see this moth on a branch, what should I look for on nearby leaves to confirm it’s causing trouble?
Q2: What leaf symptoms near this moth on the branch would indicate it is responsible for damage?
label: Look for irregular notches, holes, or skeletonized tissue on new spring growth—especially tender leaves and shoot tips. Western tussock moth larvae preferentially feed on expanding foliage; heavy feeding can strip entire shoots bare, leaving only midribs. Also check for tiny black caterpillars (early stage) or larger larvae with red/yellow spots and four gray dorsal hair tufts. Damage often appears clustered near where egg masses were laid, typically on shaded bark or leaf undersides.

Q1:
<image>
The insect’s legs are firmly planted on the leaf—does that mean it’s about to lay eggs there?
Q2: Is the insect positioned on the leaf in a way that suggests imminent egg-laying?
label: No—grasshoppers lay eggs in soil, not on leaves. Females deposit egg pods (each containing 20–100 eggs) in undisturbed topsoil, typically in late summer/fall. The upright, grounded posture indicates resting or feeding readiness, not oviposition. Egg-laying behavior involves digging into dry soil with the ovipositor (abdomen tip), which is not observed here. This individual is likely a nymph or adult foraging; monitor soil near field borders for future egg pods if populations persist.

Q1:
<image>
In Figure 125, circular brown scars are visible on the fruit surface, resembling a constricted band. Is this related to the small holes observed on the leaves?
Q2: Do the circular brown, band-like scars on the fruit in Figure 125 correspond to the small holes present on the leaves?
label: Directly related—circular scars result from tea thrips nymphs aggregating and piercing the pedicel or stylar end of young fruits during early fruit development (when diameter < 1.5 cm). Thrips prefer to feed in concealed areas near the base of sepals, causing epidermal cell necrosis and suberization. As the fruit enlarges, these wounds are stretched into concentric ‘rust rings’. Meanwhile, small punctures on leaves (as shown in Figure 124) represent concurrent feeding damage by the same nymph population on tender leaves, reflecting the dispersal trajectory of the same pest cohort. In the field, simultaneous inspection can be conducted: remove affected fruits, peel back tissues beneath the calyx, and if orange-yellow elongated nymphs (0.8–1.2 mm in length) are found, the causal relationship is confirmed.

Q1:
<image>
The bug’s legs have red-orange joints—is that a sign it’s recently fed or just its natural color?
Q2: Do the red-orange leg joints on the insect indicate recent feeding, or are they part of its natural coloration?
label: The red-orange coloration at leg joints is a stable morphological trait, not a feeding indicator. In *Anoplocnemis* and related edge bugs, these markings are genetically determined and persist regardless of feeding status. A recently fed bug would show a distended, darker abdomen (due to ingested sap), not leg-color changes. To assess recent feeding, examine the abdomen: if translucent and swollen with amber fluid, it likely fed recently; if flat and opaque, it may be fasting or pre-oviposition. No such abdominal swelling is visible here.

Q1:
<image>
I found bugs like this on the edge of my field—what’s the quickest low-risk way to stop them before they hit crops?
Q2: What is the fastest, safest method to control these insects located at the field edge before they reach the crops?
label: Apply bait-based biocontrol *now*, while nymphs are still small and聚集 (aggregated). Use Nosema asiaticus spore-treated wheat bran bait (1×10¹² spores/kg) at 5–10 kg/ha along the infested border strip (10–20 m wide). The bait exploits their ground-foraging behavior: infected nymphs stop feeding within 3–5 days, reducing crop damage and spreading disease to others. Avoid broad-spectrum sprays—they kill natural enemies (e.g., birds, robber flies) and may trigger resistance. Recheck in 5 days; if >30% remain active, reapply bait or spot-treat with spinosad (low bee risk) on border only.

Q1:
<image>
Are the black spots on this leaf indicative of black spot disease? How can one identify it?
Q2: Do the black spots visible on this leaf confirm black spot disease, and what visual features distinguish it?
label: This represents typical symptoms of black spot disease. Multiple irregular dark brown to black spots are visible in the image, with slightly yellowish halos around their edges, concentrated primarily in the lower to middle portions of the leaf surface. Localized chlorosis surrounds the lesions, and leaf margins show mild curling and damage—consistent with early to intermediate stages of infection by Alternaria alternata, a species of the genus Alternaria. Compared to Septoria spot, which features smaller, rounder, often sunken lesions commonly found on fruits, the current lesions are larger, irregularly shaped, lack obvious depression, and occur on leaves, supporting a diagnosis of black spot disease.

Q1:
<image>
Why do leaves affected by Huanglongbing sometimes appear merely yellow, resembling symptoms of nutrient deficiency?
Q2: What causes the yellowing of leaves in Huanglongbing, which can mimic nutrient deficiency symptoms?
label: Huanglongbing can manifest as "uniform chlorosis," resembling nitrogen or iron deficiency due to disruption of phloem transport leading to disordered distribution of photosynthates and nutrients. However, a key distinction lies in reversibility: nutrient deficiency symptoms can be reversed upon fertilization, whereas HLB-induced chlorosis is irreversible. Moreover, HLB is often accompanied by leaf thickening, hardened petioles, shortened new shoots, and fruit exhibiting “red nose” symptoms. Field verification involves cutting suspected branches and observing whether newly emerged leaves show a characteristic yellow-green mottling pattern—a visual hallmark with the highest diagnostic value for HLB.

Q1:
<image>
The hard, black-green nodules on the two forked stems on the right feel firm—have they already formed scabs? Is further spread likely?
Q2: Do the firm, black-green nodules on the two forked stems on the right indicate scab formation, and is additional spread probable?
label: These dark greenish-black small protrusions are not scabs but rather aggregates of fungal hyphae or microfructifications formed by pathogens such as Fusarium solani on the stem surface—firm in texture and firmly attached. Their distribution along the stem axis, especially concentrated near nodes, indicates that the disease has already advanced from the roots upward into the basal stem region. If left unmanaged, the lesion will spread upward via vascular bundles, obstructing nutrient and water transport in upper branches, leading to leaf chlorosis, shortened new shoots, reduced fruit set, and eventually death of entire branches. On-site, a few of these protrusions can be scraped off and placed on a moist filter paper for 24 hours; if white, fluffy hyphae develop, this provides preliminary confirmation of a fungal etiology.

Q1:
<image>
After discovering such insects, should we apply pesticides first, or should we first check for natural enemies?
Q2: Upon observing these insects, is it advisable to apply pesticides immediately, or should natural enemies be assessed first?
label: First, assess natural enemies: use a hand lens to inspect the insect’s surface or interior for parasitoid eggs (tiny oval white spots), larvae (semi-transparent crawling forms), or emergence holes (small circular openings); also check for activity of ladybird beetle larvae, lacewing larvae, or adult parasitoids on either leaf surface. *Coccus hesperidum* has abundant natural enemies (e.g., *Delphastus pusillus*, *Metaphycus angustifrons*). If parasitism rates exceed 30% or predators are active, postpone chemical treatment and instead use yellow sticky traps to disrupt ant activity and minimize human disturbance. Apply targeted spraying only when pest density increases rapidly (e.g., >50% increase within 3 days) and natural enemies are absent, using 1.8% abamectin emulsion directly at the junction of leaf back and midrib to avoid non-target killing of beneficial organisms.

Q1:
<image>
Why are these insects concentrated on the upper half of the stem, and why is there no visible sign of movement?
Q2: Why are the insects clustered on the upper portion of the stem and appear motionless?
label: Due to the brief crawling phase of newly hatched nymphs seeking suitable attachment sites, once a position is selected, they secrete wax to firmly anchor and cease movement. The upper stem segment, receiving ample sunlight and rich in succulent tissue, is preferred for settlement. The immobile attachment of the insect in the image, with no traces of dragging or shed exuviae, indicates it has entered a stable feeding stage (typically after the second instar), not a recently arrived population. Additionally, check for ant activity—honeydew attracts ants, which may drive away natural enemies and protect scale insects, thereby exacerbating local aggregation.

Q1:
<image>
This yellow fruit has many tiny black specks on the skin—could this be black spot disease?
Q2: Does the yellow fruit in the image show numerous small black specks on its skin?
label: Yes, the scattered small dark brown to black speckles on a mature yellow fruit surface are consistent with early-stage Alternaria black spot (caused by Alternaria alternata). However, definitive diagnosis requires checking for sunken lesions or black pycnidia (tiny raised dots) under magnification; Septoria spot may also cause similar speckling but typically appears as slightly depressed tan-to-black spots that enlarge in storage. Visual evidence alone supports suspicion but not confirmation.

Q1:
<image>
Does this look like nutrient deficiency or a disease? The yellow area isn’t between veins and there’s a dark speck too.
Q2: Is the yellowing in this image due to nutrient deficiency or disease, given that it occurs outside the veins and includes a dark speck?
label: This is more consistent with Huanglongbing than nutrient deficiency. In zinc or iron deficiency, yellowing occurs *between* veins (interveinal chlorosis) and is usually symmetrical; here, the yellow patch is irregular, unilateral, and associated with a brown vascular streak—classic HLB mottling. The small dark speck may be a necrotic spot from secondary infection or minor physical injury, but not diagnostic alone. HLB symptoms persist despite fertilizer application, unlike true deficiencies.

Q1:
<image>
How will this circular lesion—featuring a yellow halo surrounding a darker center—progress further on the leaf?
Q2: What is the likely progression of this circular leaf lesion with a yellow halo and darker central area?
label: These spots are typically initiated by fungal invasion through stomata or minor wounds, beginning with a latent phase (visible only as a yellow halo), followed by central necrosis turning brown and expanding into near-circular lesions. Under persistently high humidity, gray-white mold layers (conidial masses) may develop along the lesion margins; later stages may result in complete desiccation, perforation, or coalescence of spots leading to premature leaf drop. It is recommended to examine the lesion center under magnification for pinpoint black dots (conidiomata), or gently rub the affected area to check for powdery residue detachment, to confirm the progression stage.

Q1:
<image>
Could heavy rain last week cause spots like these to appear suddenly?
Q2: Did recent heavy rainfall trigger the sudden appearance of these spots?
label: Yes—rain is a primary driver: Xanthomonas citri requires a continuous leaf-wetness period of ≥20 minutes for successful infection through stomata or wounds. Heavy rain not only provides the necessary moisture film but also splashes bacteria from existing lesions onto healthy tissue. If the tree had latent infections or nearby infected trees, last week’s rain could have triggered this visible outbreak. However, without prior inoculum source (e.g., infected trees, contaminated tools), rain alone wouldn’t cause it—so check for nearby symptomatic trees or recent pruning activity.

Q1:
<image>
Does the insect in the photo have features that rule out it being a cricket or katydid?
Q2: Based on the image, does the insect display characteristics inconsistent with those of crickets or katydids?
label: Yes. Crickets and katydids have antennae significantly longer than their body length, while this insect’s antennae are only slightly longer than its head—typical of grasshoppers. Also, its hind tibiae bear dense spines (visible in image), and the body lacks the elongated ovipositor of female katydids or the sound-producing file-and-scraper structures of crickets. The compact, robust build and folded forewings further support grasshopper classification.

Q1:
<image>
A citrus leaf exhibits asymmetric, blotchy chlorosis with distinct green islands, no evidence of arthropod feeding, stippling, necrosis, or epidermal collapse—what is the most likely diagnosis consistent with these visual symptoms?
Q2: What disease is indicated by asymmetric, blotchy yellowing on a citrus leaf with preserved green areas, in the absence of insect damage, stippling, tissue death, or surface collapse?
label: The most likely diagnosis is Huanglongbing (HLB), also known as citrus greening disease, caused by Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus. This diagnosis is supported by the hallmark visual symptom of asymmetric, blotchy chlorosis—where yellowed areas irregularly intermingle with retained green tissue forming 'green islands'—a pathognomonic pattern resulting from phloem sieve tube dysfunction and uneven carbohydrate accumulation. The absence of stippling, necrotic lesions, epidermal collapse, or physical damage rules out biotic agents such as mites, aphids, or fungal pathogens, and confirms that the discoloration is systemic and phloem-limited rather than localized or abiotic in origin.

Q1:
<image>
Can I spray something now since the grasshopper is alone and plants look fine?
Q2: Is there any immediate treatment needed given the solitary grasshopper presence and absence of visible plant damage?
label: No—chemical control is unjustified at this stage. Spraying a solitary adult risks killing predators (e.g., birds, robber flies) and selecting for resistance without preventing damage. Instead, use cultural tactics: mow or till 5–10 m wide buffer strips around fields before adjacent vegetation dries, removing egg-laying sites and food sources. If nymphs appear, prioritize targeted bait application over foliar sprays; malathion (if used) should only cover border zones, not entire orchards, to conserve natural enemies.

Q1:
<image>
There's a small black spot on this leaf, resembling a tiny beetle resting on the surface—what kind of insect is it?
Q2: What insect is depicted as a small black spot on the leaf surface in this image?
label: This small black spot is an adult gray longhorn beetle (Pantomorus cervinus), identified by its size (approximately 1–2 mm), dark oval shape, stationary position on leaf surfaces, and characteristic irregularly notched leaf margins. Combined with the background of citrus trees and symptoms of damage on new shoots and tender leaves, this strongly confirms it as gray longhorn beetle rather than other leaf beetles or flea beetles. The insect is wingless with a short rostrum and typically rests on leaf surfaces during early morning hours or on overcast days.

Q1:
<image>
This leaf has dark brown to black irregular spots—could this be citrus canker?
Q2: Does this leaf exhibit dark brown to black irregular spots indicative of citrus canker?
label: Yes, the dark brown to black irregular, well-defined but occasionally coalesced spots on the upper surface of a green citrus leaf are highly consistent with early-to-mid stage citrus canker (caused by Xanthomonas citri subsp. citri). The absence of raised pustules or corky margins in this image suggests it may be pre-rupture or early necrotic phase; confirmation requires checking the leaf underside for oil-soaked halos or bacterial exudate under magnification.

Q1:
<image>
Does the presence of asymmetric, interveinal chlorosis with distinct green islands retained along the midrib and primary veins—particularly near the leaf apex—indicate early-stage Huanglongbing infection?
Q2: Does this leaf show asymmetric, interveinal yellowing with green tissue preserved along the midrib and primary veins, especially toward the tip?
label: Yes, this pattern is a hallmark visual indicator of early-stage Huanglongbing, caused by Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus. The asymmetric interveinal chlorosis reflects phloem dysfunction and starch accumulation in mesophyll cells, while the persistent green islands along the midrib and major veins result from localized resistance to phloem sieve tube occlusion and uneven bacterial distribution. Unlike nutrient deficiencies or abiotic stress, which typically produce symmetrical or marginal chlorosis, Huanglongbing-induced chlorosis is characteristically blotchy, unilaterally distributed, and associated with vein-associated green retention—a direct morphological correlate of systemic phloem-limited pathogen colonization.

Q1:
<image>
The leaf shows no insects or wounds—where did this black spot come from?
Q2: What is the origin of the black spot on this leaf, given the absence of insects or wounds?
label: This dark spot is likely an initial infection site formed after bacteria entered through stomata or minor wounds: Xanthomonas citri can penetrate into host tissues via stomata or lenticels under moist conditions with a continuous water film lasting more than 20 minutes, even without visible injuries. No signs of insect damage or mechanical injury are observed in the image; however, residual moisture films are evident on the leaf surface (uneven glossiness, localized weak reflectivity). Combined with the background of hot and rainy seasons, this scenario aligns with the natural invasion pathway of bacterial pathogens. Wind-induced abrasions or salt crystallization from dew evaporation must also be ruled out, though the latter typically does not lead to progressive lesion development.

Q1:
<image>
The discolored area on the fruit looks rough and split open—what does that tell us about how far the disease has gone?
Q2: What does the rough, split appearance of the discolored area on the fruit indicate about the disease progression?
label: The rough, cracked appearance indicates the lesion has entered the late stage of citrus canker development: the initial water-soaked spot has become elevated, formed a spongy pustule, then necrotized and corked, leading to surface rupture. To verify in the field, gently scrape the lesion with a fingernail—if it feels hard and woody (not soft/mushy), and the crack reveals dry, brown tissue beneath, it confirms advanced木栓化 (corking). This stage means the pathogen is no longer actively spreading *within* the fruit, but the damage is irreversible and the fruit is unmarketable.

Q1:
<image>
The insect is alone on the leaf, and no other insects are visible—does this mean the damage this year is not severe?
Q2: Is the absence of other insects on the leaf, with only this one present, indicative of low-severity damage this year?
label: The presence of a single larva does not indicate low population density. Adult Bactrocera minax females lay eggs covertly (under the fruit skin), and after hatching, larvae burrow into the flesh—making live individuals difficult to detect in the field until they mature and exit the fruit. One larva usually corresponds to one infested fruit, while a single female can lay 100–200 eggs. Therefore, assessment should be based on the number of fallen fruits: if ≥5 fallen fruits are found per tree within the same period, the infestation rate may exceed 10%, representing a threshold requiring intervention. It is recommended to conduct continuous inspections of fallen fruits for three consecutive days and record findings.

Q1:
<image>
These insects are clinging to the leaves, with black spots around them and whitish spots on the leaf tissue—how would the leaves appear in response?
Q2: What visual changes are evident on the leaf tissue where these insects are attached, given the presence of black spots around them and whitish spots on the leaves?
label: Leaves will exhibit localized chlorosis, yellowing, or necrotic spots, accompanied by black sooty mold lesions (induced by honeydew) and bright white linear crawling marks. In severe cases, the leaf surface becomes glossy and sticky, heavily covered with black mold, leading to reduced photosynthesis and ultimately causing premature defoliation. Verification method: gently rub the black spots with a finger—if they wipe off easily and leave an oily residue, it indicates sooty mold. Under magnification, small piercing-sucking mouthparts can be observed embedded in the tissue beneath the insects, often corresponding to minute depressions or necrotic rings.

Q1:
<image>
In this image, a cluster of white-tipped, swollen galls is visible on a young citrus branch; the surrounding leaves show no chlorosis, necrosis, or stippling—do these galls exhibit diagnostic morphological features consistent with Contarinia citri infestation, such as conical shape, epidermal rupture exposing creamy-white larval bodies, and presence of cast larval exuviae at the gall apex?
Q2: Does this image show white-tipped, swollen galls on a young citrus branch that are conical, ruptured at the epidermis to expose creamy-white larval bodies, and topped with cast larval exuviae—without chlorosis, necrosis, or stippling in surrounding leaves?
label: Yes, these galls are diagnostic of Contarinia citri, the citrus gall midge. The white tips correspond to immature galls where the epidermis has not yet ruptured, but their conical morphology, uniform swelling at apical meristems of new shoots, and pale translucency indicate active larval feeding beneath intact epidermis. As development progresses, the epidermis undergoes localized collapse and fissuring, revealing creamy-white third-instar larvae and often retaining cast exuviae—key visual hallmarks distinguishable from abiotic tip dieback or other gall-inducing pests. The absence of foliar symptoms confirms that damage is confined to meristematic tissue, aligning with Contarinia citri’s obligate endophytic behavior in tender shoot apices.

Q1:
<image>
Is the yellowish patch next to the insect possibly where it has bitten? The edge is irregular, and the color transitions gradually from yellow to green. The area feels somewhat dry when touched.
Q2: Does the irregular, yellow-to-green transitional patch adjacent to the insect exhibit dry texture?
label: Yes, this yellowing area is very likely an initial injury caused by feeding activity of the citrus leaf beetle. Adults use chewing mouthparts to consume leaf mesophyll, resulting in localized tissue necrosis and degradation of chlorophyll, manifesting as irregular yellow spots with blurred margins due to patchy expansion from feeding; upon flipping the leaf underside, small notches or punctures are often visible in corresponding areas. It is recommended to immediately inspect the undersides of newly emerged shoots on the same branch for similar lesions or residual insect bodies.

Q1:
<image>
We’ve found one leaf exhibiting this yellowing—should we spray pesticides now, or should we consider cutting down the tree first?
Q2: Given this single leaf showing yellowing, is immediate pesticide application warranted, or is tree removal the more appropriate action?
label: Isolated leaf abnormalities are still in the monitoring phase and should not prompt immediate tree removal. Priority actions should be: ① mark the affected branch and recheck within 7 days to see if chlorosis has spread to three or more leaves on the same branch; ② use a magnifier to inspect the leaf undersides and tender shoots for citrus psyllid eggs or nymphs (focus on curled leaf margins); ③ if psyllids are confirmed, immediately spray the entire orchard with imidacloprid or thiamethoxam (targeting new shoots and leaf undersides). Only when PCR confirms infection and multiple branches show symptoms should the infected trees be completely uprooted.

Q1:
<image>
If I see more leaves like this in my orchard, what’s the first thing I should do—not spray, but inspect?
Q2: What should I inspect first—not treat—if I observe additional leaves with this appearance in my orchard?
label: First, examine the *undersides* of 5–10 similar leaves under bright light or with a 10× hand lens for minute raised spots or oil-like lesions—especially near the midrib or margin. Second, check adjacent new shoots for lesions, as canker starts on tender tissue. Third, verify soil moisture and recent fertilizer history. Only if lesions are confirmed should you consider copper sprays on new growth; otherwise, correct nutrition/irrigation. Early misdiagnosis leads to unnecessary spraying.

Q1:
<image>
Could this fruit problem come from a virus instead of a bacterial disease?
Q2: Is this fruit symptom likely caused by a viral infection rather than a bacterial one?
label: Unlikely—citrus viruses (e.g., Citrus tristeza virus) typically cause stem-pitting, vein clearing, or uniform fruit drop, not unilateral rind browning with deformation. The observed asymmetry, small aborted seeds, and vascular browning point strongly to *Candidatus* Liberibacter asiaticus, a phloem-limited bacterium. Viruses are usually transmitted by aphids or grafting and lack the characteristic ‘red nose’ fruit phenotype. Molecular testing is definitive, but visually, bacterial etiology is far more probable.

Q1:
<image>
The leaf edge is brown and curled inward—what does that tell us about how far the disease has progressed?
Q2: What does the brown, inwardly curled leaf margin indicate about the disease's progression?
label: Curling plus marginal browning indicates moderate to advanced infection: the pathogen has colonized mesophyll tissue, causing cell death and loss of turgor. At this stage, lesions are likely expanding beyond the initial spot phase; check the underside for gray-green fungal growth (conidia), which confirms active sporulation and high risk of secondary spread. Compare with healthy leaves—if newer leaves show similar spots, the disease is actively progressing.

Q1:
<image>
If I find moths like this resting on tree trunks in spring, what leaf symptoms should I look for next?
Q2: What leaf symptoms are associated with the presence of moths like this resting on tree trunks during spring?
label: Look for newly flushed terminals with tightly rolled or folded leaves held by silk, often with transparent 'window-feeding' patches where leaf tissue is eaten but upper epidermis remains intact; older larvae may tie leaves to young fruit, causing entry wounds. Inspect the underside of curled terminals—live green caterpillars with black heads are usually hidden inside. Damage appears 1–2 weeks after moth emergence, coinciding with spring flush.

Q1:
<image>
What kind of insect is responsible for the translucent, small circular spots on the leaves, which appear darker in the center and bulge upward like a lid?
Q2: Which insect causes small, circular, translucent leaf spots that are darker centrally and elevated like a lid?
label: Yes, this is either a female adult or nymph of the red wax scale. The identification is based on: a circular, dome-shaped body covered by a translucent to pale yellow-brown waxy shell, with a dark central umbilicus (representing the mouthparts and molt remnants) tightly adhered to both sides of the main leaf vein; no legs, antennae, or other locomotive structures are visible—consistent with the sessile feeding habit of scale insects. Compared to the brown soft scale, its wax covering is thicker and more convex, lacking distinct annular patterns or mottled color patches.

Q1:
<image>
If I see this on a few leaves in my grove, should I spray the whole block or just the affected tree?
Q2: Based on this image, is treatment required for the entire block or only the individual tree showing these symptoms?
label: Do not spray the whole block yet. First, isolate and test the affected tree; if confirmed HLB-positive, remove it entirely (including roots) immediately—this is the most effective control. Then, apply targeted insecticide sprays (e.g., neonicotinoids like acetamiprid) only to the perimeter rows and any trees within 30 meters, focusing on new flush where psyllids feed. Whole-block spraying is unnecessary and risks resistance; instead, monitor psyllid populations weekly and treat only when nymphs exceed threshold (e.g., >1 per 10 shoots).

Q1:
<image>
If I spray copper now on a tree like this—full of clean-looking fruit and green leaves—will it help stop black spot before it starts?
Q2: Will applying copper spray to this tree—displaying healthy-looking fruit and green leaves—prevent black spot from developing?
label: Copper sprays are effective *preventively* against black spot, but timing matters: apply *before* infection occurs, ideally after petal fall and during early fruit expansion, or after rain events in high-risk periods (July–Sept). Spraying now on symptom-free fruit is low-risk and may help, but prioritize canopy thinning first. For organic systems, fixed copper + lime (Bordeaux mix) is acceptable; for conventional, consider azoxystrobin/difenoconazole if resistance management is needed. Always avoid spraying during bloom or extreme heat.

Q1:
<image>
Why do these tiny insects cluster in the grooves along the leaf veins instead of staying on the flat surfaces?
Q2: Why are these small insects聚集 along the leaf vein grooves rather than on the flat leaf surfaces?
label: The vein grooves provide physical shelter (reducing desiccation and exposure to natural enemies), concentrate moisture and nutrients (due to high phloem sap concentration), and offer stable anchoring points for sustained feeding. Apple aphids exhibit a strong preference for concave microhabitats—especially pronounced on tender leaves where they tend to align along the midvein. Furthermore, the flattened, adherent posture of the aphids in the image indicates adaptation to narrow crevices, reflecting long-term co-evolutionary selection for optimal feeding microenvironments, rather than random attachment.

Q1:
<image>
Is this white structure a fungus, an insect larva, or just leaf damage?
Q2: Does this white feature represent fungal growth, an insect larva, or physical leaf injury?
label: It is an insect larval mine, specifically from citrus leafminer, not a fungus or abiotic damage. Key visual evidence: (1) the structure follows a non-vascular, meandering path with branching; (2) it is raised slightly above the surface, indicating internal excavation; (3) the dense terminal mass corresponds to the pupal chamber where the larva rolls the leaf edge. Fungal hyphae would be finer, non-raised, and often associated with discoloration; abiotic damage (e.g., mechanical scarring) would lack this organized, self-contained tunneling pattern.

Q1:
<image>
I found this kind of insect on the field ridge—should I spray pesticide now, or should I observe it first?
Q2: Is immediate pesticide application necessary for this insect observed on the field ridge, or is monitoring sufficient?
label: Immediate pesticide application is not recommended; instead, prioritize inspecting nearby areas within 50 meters—such as wastelands and ditches—for the presence of nymphs (especially gregarious "nests" of early-stage nymphs before the second instar). If only scattered adults are observed, establish toxic bait strips (e.g., *Metarhizium acridum* spore-infused wheat bait) along field borders to prevent unintended harm to natural enemies. Systemic chemical control should only be considered when ≥5 individuals per 10 m² are detected for three consecutive days, and fresh feeding damage on young crop leaves is confirmed, with low-risk agents (e.g., malathion) applied locally (limited to perimeter spraying).

Q1:
<image>
I found one of these moths on my citrus—should I spray now or wait for signs of larvae?
Q2: Is the presence of this moth on my citrus plant sufficient reason to apply pesticide, or should I delay treatment until larval damage appears?
label: Do not spray immediately based on a single adult. Instead, begin monitoring: check upper-third twigs for gray-brown egg masses before mid-March (in temperate zones), and once spring flush appears, inspect 20 random trees weekly for live caterpillars in leaf nests. Apply Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis) only when ≥20% of new terminals host live larvae—or ~400 worms/hour search time. Spraying too early wastes resources and harms beneficials; Bt must contact young, actively feeding larvae and degrades rapidly in sunlight.

Q1:
<image>
Can I use a simple trap instead of spraying if I keep spotting moths like this near my crops?
Q2: Is a simple trap sufficient to manage the moth presence visible in this image, instead of applying sprays?
label: Yes—install sex pheromone traps (one per 150 m²) with *S. exigua*-specific lure suspended 1.5 m above ground; combine with sugar-vinegar-ethanol-water bait (3:4:1:2 ratio) in shallow pans to attract and drown adults. Monitor trap catch weekly: if >5 moths/trap/week, initiate larval scouting and consider targeted spray only if larvae are found on plants.

Q1:
<image>
The spots are denser near the top right of the fruit—does that mean the infection came from above?
Q2: Is the higher concentration of spots in the top right area of the fruit indicative of an infection originating from above?
label: Yes, the higher density on the upper-right quadrant strongly suggests vertical inoculum delivery—likely rain-splashed spores from infected leaves or twigs overhead, or wind-driven spores settling on the upward-facing surface. In citrus, fruit orientation matters: the calyx end (top) often faces upward and stays wet longer, favoring spore germination; also, canopy architecture may shield the lower-left side. To test this hypothesis, check leaves directly above this fruit for similar lesions or necrotic tips, and inspect drip lines for fallen infected debris.

Q1:
<image>
I see one adult butterfly on my young citrus tree—should I spray now to stop damage?
Q2: Is there visible damage to the young citrus tree that would warrant immediate spraying due to the presence of an adult butterfly?
label: No immediate spraying is needed; adults do not feed or damage trees. Instead, monitor new shoots daily for eggs (small, round, pale yellow) or first-instar caterpillars (dark, mottled, resembling bird droppings). If eggs or small larvae are found, apply Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) to嫩梢 (new growth) when larvae are actively feeding—this targets caterpillars selectively without harming beneficial insects. Spraying at the adult stage is ineffective and unnecessary.

Q1:
<image>
Why are only the newer leaves damaged while older ones look intact?
Q2: Why do the newer leaves show damage whereas the older leaves appear unaffected?
label: Gray weevils exhibit strong趋嫩性 (preference for tender tissue); they selectively feed on newly expanded, soft leaves because they are easier to chew and richer in nutrients. Older, hardened leaves resist feeding and are avoided unless population pressure is extreme. This pattern helps diagnose early infestation: if notches appear only on current-season flush, it indicates low-to-moderate adult density targeting new growth—ideal window for cultural control before population surges.

Q1:
<image>
Is this insect a locust, with its head facing left, thick hind legs, wings folded on its back, and green body marked with red-brown stripes?
Q2: Does this insect have a green body with red-brown stripes, thick hind legs, folded wings, and a head oriented to the left?
label: It is a locust (Orthoptera: Acrididae). Evidence includes: ① the hind tibia clearly enlarged and specialized as a jumping leg; ② antennae shorter than the body length (a typical locust characteristic, distinguishing it from katydids or crickets); ③ forewings leathery and hindwings membranous, folded and covered dorsally, with pale venation and darkened wing tips; ④ body coloration consisting of protective greenish hue with a reddish-brown longitudinal stripe along the dorsal midline, consistent with the mimicry of common herbivorous locust nymphs or early adults. The individual in the image is at a late nymphal stage or early adult stage, not yet fully mature or completely molted.

Q1:
<image>
Why are these small black spots concentrated along the leaf veins, and why are they more numerous the closer they are to the main vein?
Q2: What causes the small black spots to be distributed along the leaf veins, with higher density near the main vein?
label: Newly hatched nymphs of the brown soft scale prefer to crawl along leaf veins in search of suitable feeding sites—main veins are rich in vascular bundles and sap concentration, which facilitates prolonged feeding; meanwhile, the grooves of veins provide physical shelter, reducing contact with natural enemies. The linear or clustered distribution of insect bodies along the midrib in the image directly reflects their feeding preference and sessile behavior. Nymphs typically settle in these positions before completing wax secretion, resulting in a density gradient that decreases from the midrib toward the leaf margin.

Q1:
<image>
Could poor nutrition cause this exact leaf pattern, or is it likely infectious?
Q2: Is this specific leaf pattern more likely due to nutrient deficiency or an infectious agent?
label: While zinc or iron deficiency can cause interveinal chlorosis, they typically produce symmetrical, vein-bounded yellowing—not the irregular,跨中脉不对称 (midvein-asymmetrical) mottling seen here. Also, nutrient deficiencies improve with foliar sprays, whereas HLB symptoms persist or worsen despite fertilization. Since the pattern matches HLB’s hallmark ‘blotchy mottle’ and no soil/test data suggests deficiency, an infectious cause (Candidatus Liberibacter) is more probable—but field validation via leaf-tissue nutrient analysis and PCR is required to rule out combined stress.

Q1:
<image>
Does this leaf’s shape and texture give any clue about the disease stage?
Q2: Can the leaf's shape and texture indicate the progression stage of the disease?
label: Yes—the leaf remains ovate with acute apex and slight asymmetry, and surface shows subtle undulations but no thickening or leathery rigidity, suggesting early to mid-stage HLB; advanced HLB often causes leaf stiffening, enlarged corky midribs, and upright shoot-leaf angles (zinc-deficiency-like posture), none of which are present here. To assess progression, check if adjacent young leaves show similar mottling or if petioles appear swollen—early signs of systemic spread.

Q1:
<image>
Are these black dots likely from fungus, injury, or chemical spray damage?
Q2: Do these black dots appear to be caused by fungal infection, physical injury, or chemical spray exposure?
label: Given their discrete, scattered distribution without surrounding discoloration or tissue collapse, fungal infection (e.g., Alternaria or Septoria) is most probable. Mechanical injury usually causes irregular cracks or bruising; copper injury shows uniform speckling or bleaching, often near spray lines. To distinguish: gently rub a spot—if it smudges or lifts, it may be superficial contamination; if embedded and firm, suspect fungal stromata. Humid conditions and prior leaf spotting increase fungal likelihood.

Q1:
<image>
Given visible serpentine epidermal mines with frass trails, purple discoloration of the mine margins, and associated chlorosis in young citrus stems, what is the appropriate integrated pest management response to confirm and manage citrus leafminer (Phyllocnistis citrella) infestation?
Q2: What integrated pest management actions are appropriate to confirm and address an infestation indicated by serpentine epidermal mines containing frass, purple margins along the mines, and chlorosis in young citrus stems?
label: The presence of serpentine epidermal mines—characterized by winding, translucent, white-to-purple discolored tunnels beneath the leaf or stem epidermis—along with embedded frass trails and marginal purpling indicates active citrus leafminer (Phyllocnistis citrella) larval feeding; this mining causes localized epidermal collapse and disrupts photosynthetic tissue, leading to chlorosis and secondary curling or distortion. Because citrus leafminer primarily targets tender, expanding foliage and shoots—and because systemic insecticides are ineffective against protected larvae inside mines—the appropriate response is not whole-tree spraying but rather targeted monitoring using pheromone traps, timely application of spinosad or abamectin during flush emergence, and conservation of natural enemies like parasitoid wasps (e.g., Cirrospilus spp. and Pnigalio spp.), while pruning only severely distorted terminals to reduce inoculum without stimulating excessive new growth that attracts oviposition.

Q1:
<image>
The small, whitish creatures on the stems that look like they're coated with powdered sugar—could they be rust mites?
Q2: Are the tiny, whitish, powdery-looking organisms on the stems rust mites?
label: It is an adult or nymph of the citrus rust mite (Phyllocoptruta oleivora). Evidence includes: minute body size covered with white waxy secretions (not fungal-like powder), aggregation on tender stems rather than leaf surfaces, dark spots visible on the body surface (residual chlorophyll or cellular contents left after feeding), consistent with the typical morphology and habitat preference of rust mites during early new shoot development. Unlike scale insect nymphs, it lacks a distinct protective scale structure; unlike aphid-like whitefly nymphs, it lacks caudal filaments and regularly arranged wax threads.

Q1:
<image>
The leaf edge has whitish gritty areas and a tiny black spot—will this spread to other leaves soon?
Q2: Does the whitish gritty discoloration along the leaf margin and the small black spot indicate imminent spread to adjacent leaves?
label: Yes, this lesion is likely active and can spread rapidly under favorable conditions. The black spot indicates ongoing bacterial multiplication, and the gritty margin suggests epidermal rupture releasing inoculum. In warm, humid weather, secondary spread to neighboring leaves via rain splash can occur within 3–5 days. To assess risk: check if new flushes (especially夏梢) are emerging nearby—if yes, infection pressure is high; also inspect leaf undersides for raised pustules (early canker signs). If no new lesions appear after 5 dry days, spread may be contained—but assume high risk until proven otherwise.

Q1:
<image>
If I see just one leaf like this on a young citrus tree, what’s the first thing I should do?
Q2: What is the immediate action required upon observing a single leaf with this appearance on a young citrus tree?
label: Immediately remove and destroy the infected leaf (burn or bag-and-trash—do not compost), then inspect nearby new flushes for similar spots. Apply a copper-based protectant (e.g., 0.5% Bordeaux mixture or 77% hydrogen oxide copper at 600×) to the entire tree, focusing on new shoots and undersides of leaves, especially within 24–48 hours after removal. This prevents secondary spread during wet periods. Do not prune heavily yet—only eliminate visibly infected tissue to avoid creating new wounds.

Q1:
<image>
This moth has a mottled wing coloration without distinct stripes or eye spots—could it be the adult stage of a leaf-rolling pest?
Q2: Does this moth, exhibiting mottled wing coloration and lacking stripes or eye spots, represent the adult form of a leaf-rolling pest?
label: Yes, this is an adult belonging to the family Tortricidae, most likely the omnivorous leafroller. Evidence: absence of eye spots and transverse bands, predominant coloration of mottled gray-brown to pale yellowish-brown, and a pale costal spot on the forewing—all consistent with typical morphological traits of the genus Platynota. In contrast to the orange tortrix (Orange Tortrix), which exhibits more uniform orange-brown ground color and more regular patterning, this specimen shows more fragmented markings and greater color contrast, supporting identification as P. stultana.

Q1:
<image>
Why are only the upper leaves damaged while lower ones look fine?
Q2: Why do the upper leaves show damage but the lower leaves appear unaffected?
label: Adult gray weevils exhibit strong趋嫩性 (preference for tender tissue) and aggregate on newly flushed terminals in the upper canopy where light and nutrients favor shoot expansion; lower leaves are older, tougher, and less attractive. Additionally, adults climb upward from the soil or trunk base, so upper foliage is encountered first. This vertical damage gradient is diagnostic for canopy-feeding weevils—not root-feeding larvae or soil-borne pathogens.

Q1:
<image>
If this bug is found on a leaf in late summer, should I spray right away or wait?
Q2: Is immediate spraying necessary upon observing this insect on a leaf during late summer?
label: Wait—late summer is peak second-generation egg-laying (June–August), so immediate spraying may miss newly laid eggs. First, inspect leaf undersides for chalky-covered egg masses; if >1 per tree, apply acetamiprid (Assail) or cyantraniliprole (Exirel) to kill nymphs emerging in 10–14 days. Avoid pyrethroids (e.g., beta-cyfluthrin) unless thrips are absent, as they induce resistance. For organic systems, use Pyganic + narrow-range oil every 10–14 days. Always confirm with yellow sticky cards: treat only if catches exceed regional action thresholds.

Q1:
<image>
In three citrus stem images showing progressive yellowing (chlorosis), discrete brown to grayish necrotic spots with irregular margins, and longitudinal epidermal cracking that exposes fibrous, discolored vascular and cortical tissues, what diagnostic features collectively confirm citrus brown rot caused by Phytophthora citrophthora or Phytophthora parasitica?
Q2: What diagnostic features are visible in three citrus stem images showing progressive yellowing, discrete brown to grayish necrotic spots with irregular margins, and longitudinal epidermal cracking that exposes fibrous, discolored vascular and cortical tissues?
label: The diagnosis of citrus brown rot is confirmed by the triad of chlorotic stem discoloration progressing from green to pale yellow, sharply demarcated necrotic lesions exhibiting brown-to-gray surface stippling and subtle mycelial matting under high-magnification inspection, and longitudinal epidermal collapse leading to deep fissures that expose desiccated, fibrous internal tissues with visible vascular browning—features pathognomonic for Phytophthora-induced stem canker and rot, distinct from abiotic cracking or bacterial stem blight due to the absence of ooze, water-soaking, or systemic wilting beyond the lesion margin.

Q1:
<image>
Does the presence of multiple adult Eurydema rugulosa (a species of stink bug in the family Pentatomidae) on the abaxial surface of a citrus leaf—characterized by distinct brown-and-orange dorsal coloration, intact exoskeletons, and tarsi firmly appressed to the leaf epidermis without visible stylet insertion or salivary sheaths—indicate active phloem feeding, or is this morphology consistent with quiescent resting behavior?
Q2: Are the observed adult Eurydema rugulosa on the underside of the citrus leaf actively feeding on phloem, or are they in a resting state, based solely on their brown-and-orange dorsal coloration, intact exoskeletons, and tarsi firmly attached to the leaf surface without visible stylet insertion or salivary sheaths?
label: This morphology is consistent with quiescent resting behavior rather than active phloem feeding. Active feeding by Eurydema rugulosa would require visible insertion of the elongated, needle-like stylets into vascular tissue, typically accompanied by subtle epidermal collapse at the puncture site, localized chlorosis radiating from feeding points, or the presence of translucent salivary sheaths extending from the mouthparts into the mesophyll—none of which are discernible in the image. Instead, the insects exhibit fully extended, non-retracted tarsi adhering to the leaf surface, symmetrical dorsal orientation, absence of abdominal flexion associated with stylet probing, and no evidence of honeydew excretion or necrotic stippling on adjacent leaf tissue—all hallmarks of behavioral quiescence. Furthermore, the intact, unbroken cuticle and lack of feeding-induced cellular disruption confirm that no current phloem ingestion is occurring.

Q1:
<image>
Why are only some leaves damaged while others nearby are untouched?
Q2: Why do some leaves show damage while adjacent leaves remain unaffected?
label: Gray weevils strongly prefer tender, newly expanded leaves on current-season shoots, especially those in the 'turning-green' phase; older leaves remain intact because their tougher texture deters feeding. The undamaged leaves in the background appear mature and slightly mottled—consistent with prior stress or aging—not resistance. Additionally, adults aggregate on specific shoots, leading to patchy damage within a cluster. This selectivity explains why damage is localized despite proximity to healthy tissue.

Q1:
<image>
The dark surface beneath the insect appears slightly moist and shiny—does this indicate it's already damaged or diseased?
Q2: Is the dark surface under the insect moist and shiny, suggesting prior damage or disease?
label: The dark, glossy, moist appearance on the surface is a typical sign of honeydew accumulation, resulting from the excretion of sugary waste after black scale feeds on sap. While honeydew itself is harmless, it attracts ants and flies and provides a nutrient substrate for sooty mold fungi, which can form a black, velvety fungal layer on leaf surfaces within days, obstructing photosynthesis. To assess risk, gently wipe the surface with a tissue: if sticky residue remains and turns black upon drying, it indicates early signs of honeydew accumulation and sooty mold development, requiring prompt intervention.

Q1:
<image>
These damaged areas vary in color, some transparent and others brown—what do the different colors indicate?
Q2: What do the varying colors—some transparent, others brown—in the damaged areas signify?
label: The transparent regions represent early mines created shortly after larval feeding, where mesophyll tissue has not yet fully died, leading to translucency due to loss of cell sap. The brown areas indicate older mines where tissue has already died and undergone oxidative browning, often accompanied by secondary infections (e.g., invasion by citrus canker bacteria). In the field, leaf texture can be assessed by gently pinching: transparent zones feel soft and elastic, while browned areas are brittle and easily broken. The coexistence of new and old mines indicates ongoing infestation; thus, other tender leaves on the same branch should be inspected for signs of new mine initiation points.

Q1:

The entire leaf appears pale yellow, yet the midrib still retains some green. Is this due to nutrient deficiency or a disease? How can it be quickly distinguished on-site?
Q2: What is the cause of uniform leaf yellowing with green midrib retention—nutrient deficiency or disease—and how can it be differentiated visually in the field?
label: This yellowing pattern represents 'asymmetric chlorosis': alternating yellow and green areas distributed along the midrib but unevenly on both sides, without typical deficiency spots (such as the inverted-V-shaped yellow patches seen in zinc deficiency or interveinal chlorosis in iron deficiency), suggesting early-stage HLB symptoms. Field verification can be rapidly conducted through: ① checking whether other leaves on the same branch also show similar asymmetric yellowing (HLB typically affects one branch first); ② inspecting the leaf undersides for nymphs of citrus psyllid (flat, pale yellow, hidden in tender shoots); ③ observing whether new shoots are short, upright, and with shortened internodes. If two out of these three criteria are met, the likelihood of HLB is high. In contrast, correcting nutrient deficiency by applying the appropriate fertilizer should result in improvement within 2–4 weeks; HLB-related yellowing will not respond to such treatment.

Q1:
<image>
Are these fruits ‘red nose’ type? They’re yellow at the stem end but still green at the tip.
Q2: Do these fruits show the 'red nose' pattern, with yellowing at the stem end while remaining green at the tip?
label: Yes—this is classic HLB 'color inversion': the peduncle (stem) end turns orange/yellow prematurely while the stylar (blossom) end remains green, creating a lopsided, asymmetrical appearance. True 'red nose' refers to reddish discoloration near the stem on some cultivars, but the key diagnostic is the mismatched ripening pattern combined with small size and bitter taste. Cut open to confirm brown vascular bundles near the stem end.

Q1:

The whitish area along the leaf margin, resembling dusted powder, is it likely to spread further? How can we confirm whether the disease is progressing?

Check the corresponding position on the leaf underside—if raised pustules or sunken spots appear simultaneously, this confirms active disease progression. Additionally, if similar tiny black spots are observed on newly emerging tender leaves adjacent to healthy ones, it indicates the disease has entered the dissemination phase.

While absence of plant tissue prevents direct symptom assessment, this species is always considered high-risk due to its role as a vector of Xylella fastidiosa and its feeding damage on citrus, grapes, and ornamentals.

This matches the database description of “visible black fecal droppings and bright white linear trails” on fruit surfaces, though no cottony egg sacs are observed in this image—indicating the insect has not yet entered peak oviposition and remains in the active feeding phase. This morphology aligns with the typical appearance of *Icerya purchasi* nymphs or females, allowing exclusion of species with distinct waxy shells (such as red wax scale) or prominent cottony egg sacs (such as ovipositing cottony cushion scales).

Q1:
<image>
This leaf has dark brown to black spots mostly near the tip and upper side—could this be citrus canker?
Q2: Does this leaf exhibit dark brown to black spots concentrated near the tip and on the upper surface?
label: Yes, the pattern matches citrus canker (caused by Xanthomonas citri subsp. citri): multiple discrete to coalesced dark brown/black necrotic spots concentrated on the upper leaf surface near the apex, with intact margins and no insect presence. These are typical early-to-mid stage lesions before corky elevation or pustule formation; confirmation requires checking the underside for raised, spongy centers or using PCR/ELISA. Confidence is high because spot distribution, color, and absence of insect damage align with bacterial canker—not fungal spots (which often have concentric rings) or insect feeding (which shows holes or frass).

Q1:

The leaf edges are curled and darkened, but there are no spots visible on the upper surface—could this be caused by that white insect?
Q2: Are the curled and darkened leaf margins associated with the presence of the white insect visible in the image?
label: Yes, this is plausible. Rust mites congregate to feed on epidermal cells of leaf undersides; initially, only faint grayish or pale yellow spots appear on the underside (barely visible to the naked eye), while the upper surface remains smooth and symptom-free. As infestation intensifies, the leaf underside becomes chlorotic and turns brown, causing the leaf to curl backward with dried, darkened margins—exactly matching the observed symptoms: leaf edge curling plus darkening without lesions on the upper surface, which corresponds to early to intermediate stages of rust mite damage. It is advised to invert the leaf and examine the underside under a 10x magnifier for silvery-gray patches or tiny moving individuals.

Q1:

Why are these insects concentrated in the central-right area of the leaf, and why are some of them fragmented?
Q2: What explains the clustering of insects in the central-right portion of the leaf and the presence of fragmented individuals there?
label: The aggregated distribution reflects the nymphs' behavior of crawling after hatching and then settling to feed: after oviposition, nymphs undergo short-distance dispersal and preferentially settle at vein junctions (where moisture and nutrients are more abundant). Fragmented individuals are likely molt remnants or empty shells left after predation by natural enemies such as ladybugs or parasitic wasps, indicating the occurrence of natural biological control; alternatively, they may result from mechanical disturbance (e.g., spraying or wind), causing partial detachment of insect bodies.

Key visual matches: flightless adult form, uniformly brown coloration with fine short hairs, elongated oval body, prominent downward-curved snout, and large bulging eyes visible from above—distinct from similar weevils like the cribrate weevil, which has a teardrop-shaped head and closely spaced eyes. All adults are females and reproduce parthenogenetically.

label: Due to the abundant vascular bundles and higher sap concentration beneath the veins, brown soft scale nymphs preferentially settle and attach at these sites shortly after hatching. In the image, the insects are densely clustered along the midrib and extend toward the leaf tip, reflecting their inherent preference for favorable feeding locations. Furthermore, the raised vein structure provides physical shelter, reducing exposure to natural enemies. After fixation, nymphs secrete wax to form a protective layer, further enhancing stability at these sites. This distribution pattern indicates a stable feeding phase of the population, not random dispersal.

Q1:

Q2: Does the darker, blurry region in the upper-left match the same disease as the sharp black dots visible elsewhere in the image?
label: Yes, that diffuse darker zone likely represents an advanced or merging lesion of *Alternaria* black spot, where multiple small spots have coalesced into a larger necrotic area. As the disease progresses, individual spots expand radially, lose their defined margins, and merge into irregular black patches—this stage often coincides with slight tissue collapse and reduced glossiness. To verify, compare with healthy adjacent peel: the transition zone should show a faint yellow halo (indicating active margin) or no halo (older, dead tissue). This pattern suggests secondary spread within the fruit surface, possibly aided by moisture retention in that region.

Q1:

Why does only this single fruit have black spots, while the others show no signs?
Q2: Why is there black spotting on just this one fruit, with no similar discoloration visible on the others?
label: Symptom expression on a single fruit reflects local microenvironmental differences: this fruit may have experienced minor mechanical injury early on (e.g., rubbing or bird peck marks), or been exposed to prolonged dew soaking, providing entry points for pathogens; alternatively, its position may be shaded, poorly ventilated, and high in humidity—favorable conditions for spore adhesion and germination. Additionally, the pathogen has a long latent period (2–10 months), so other fruits on the same tree have not yet reached the symptomatic stage. It is recommended to inspect nearby fruits on the same branch and the undersides of leaves—if needle-point-sized black spots are already present on leaf undersides—it indicates systemic infection across the entire plant, and this fruit is merely the first case to show symptoms.

Q1:
