Why does only the center of this leaf look yellow while the edges stay green?
Q2: Why is the central portion of this leaf yellow while the margins remain green?
label: This pattern reflects early Huanglongbing infection where phloem blockage by Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus disrupts nutrient transport, causing midrib-proximal chlorosis first. To verify in field: compare this leaf with adjacent new flushes—if newer leaves show similar asymmetrical yellowing or upright posture (acute shoot-leaf angle), it strengthens HLB suspicion; also check leaf underside for thickened, corky midrib—a hallmark sign not visible here but often co-occurring.

Q1:
<image>
Is the yellowing on this leaf caused by bacteria entering through the petiole?
Q2: Does bacterial entry via the petiole cause the yellowing visible on this leaf?
label: Unlikely. Bacterial canker (Xanthomonas citri) typically enters via wounds, stomata, or hydathodes and produces distinct raised, water-soaked spots—not diffuse discoloration. Bacterial blast (Pseudomonas syringae) does infect via petiole injury and causes blackening at the base, followed by wilting and drop; here, the petiole appears intact and no blackening or girdling is visible. The absence of lesions, exudate, or tissue collapse suggests non-bacterial causes such as uneven light exposure, root stress, or micronutrient imbalance.

Q1:
<image>
This yellow-orange fruit has many tiny black specks on its skin—could this be black spot disease?
Q2: Does the presence of numerous small black specks on the yellow-orange fruit's skin indicate black spot disease?
label: Yes, the scattered small dark brown to black specks on the mature fruit surface are consistent with early-stage Alternaria black spot (caused by Alternaria alternata). Unlike Septoria spot—which typically shows sunken, larger lesions with fruiting bodies embedded in the rind—these specks are superficial, non-sunken, and evenly distributed without obvious tissue collapse, supporting a diagnosis of black spot rather than Septoria. Confirmation requires microscopic examination of spores or lesion cross-sections.

Q1:
<image>
If many leaves in the orchard are drying out like the one shown in this image, what fungicide should be applied now?
Q2: What fungicide is appropriate to apply now if numerous orchard leaves exhibit the same drying symptoms as shown in the image?
label: When a large number of leaves have already dried up, it indicates the disease has entered its late outbreak phase. Chemical control becomes ineffective on old, dry leaves; immediate implementation of three measures is essential: ① Orchard sanitation—completely remove all infected branches, leaves, and fruits, then burn them centrally to reduce overwintering inoculum sources; ② Protect new shoots—spray healthy new leaves with 75% chlorothalonil diluted 600 times or 64% fosetyl-aluminum, focusing especially on the leaf undersides, repeated 2–3 times at 7-day intervals; ③ Improve environmental conditions—prune overcrowded branches to reduce canopy density, and switch from flood irrigation to drip irrigation to manage humidity. Avoid spraying dry leaves, as this is wasteful and may induce fungicide resistance.

Q1:
<image>
When a spot like this appears on a leaf, what visible changes happen next if left untreated?
Q2: What visible progression occurs in this leaf spot if no intervention is applied?
label: Untreated, the spot will enlarge, become more raised and corky, and develop a cracked, tan-to-brown center surrounded by a yellow halo; the leaf may curl or distort due to uneven tissue death. Within 7–10 days, adjacent leaves often show new oil-soaked spots, especially on the underside, and severe cases lead to premature leaf drop—visible as scattered yellowing leaves near the branch tip.

Q1:
<image>
I caught one of these caterpillars like in the photo—should I spray the whole tree or just watch for more?
Q2: Based on the image, should the entire tree be treated with pesticide, or is monitoring for additional caterpillars sufficient?
label: One isolated larva does not warrant spraying; manually remove and destroy it, then monitor new citrus flushes every 3–5 days for eggs (small, pale spheres on leaf undersides) or small larvae. If >2–3 larvae per young tree are found, apply Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) to new growth only—targeting the leaf undersides where larvae feed—since Bt is highly effective against young caterpillars and safe for beneficial insects.

Q1:
<image>
What changes would appear on the leaves if this insect were to appear in the field?
Q2: What leaf symptoms would be visible if this insect were present in the field?
label: This insect is a piercing-sucking pest; if abundant during the tender leaf stage of jujube trees, it can cause chlorosis, leaf curling, and difficulty in leaf unfolding; young buds may shrivel, and growth of new shoots may stagnate. Field inspection should focus on whether adult insects are congregating on the underside of tender leaves, or whether irregular chlorotic spots or slight wrinkling appear on leaf surfaces. In severe cases, entire branches may desiccate; confirming the damage stage requires further assessment of oviposition scars at the base of twigs.

Q1:
<image>
Is the bug in the photo a caterpillar or a butterfly? It’s sitting on soil with green leaf bits nearby but not on a leaf.
Q2: Does the insect shown in the image resemble a caterpillar or a butterfly, given its position on soil and proximity to green leaf fragments?
label: It is a butterfly (adult stage), not a caterpillar. Visual cues: fully developed wings held upright, slender segmented body with visible antennae and six legs, no prolegs or fleshy segments typical of larvae. The presence of green leaf fragments on the ground suggests recent larval feeding nearby, but this individual is the non-feeding adult that lays eggs on new growth.

Q1:
<image>
Based on the presence of raised, corky, tan-to-brown lesions with yellow chlorotic halos and associated epidermal collapse on the adaxial surface of mature citrus leaves, along with occasional coalescing necrotic margins and occasional bacterial exudate visible under oblique lighting, does this visual presentation confirm citrus bacterial canker (Xanthomonas citri subsp. citri), and what is the appropriate spatial scope of copper-based bactericide application—targeted to symptomatic foliage only or extended to the entire canopy?
Q2: Does the image show raised, corky, tan-to-brown lesions with yellow chlorotic halos, epidermal collapse on the upper surface of mature citrus leaves, coalescing necrotic margins, and bacterial exudate visible under oblique lighting?
label: Yes, this visual presentation confirms citrus bacterial canker, caused by Xanthomonas citri subsp. citri. Diagnosis is grounded in three key morphological features observable in the image: first, the elevated, corky, tan-to-brown lesions result from hypertrophic cell proliferation and subepidermal bacterial colonization leading to epidermal rupture; second, the distinct yellow chlorotic halos reflect phytotoxin-induced disruption of chloroplast integrity and localized photosynthetic inhibition; third, the irregular necrotic margins and occasional translucent exudate under oblique illumination indicate active bacterial ooze and progressive tissue necrosis. Because citrus bacterial canker is a systemic, wind- and rain-splashed pathogen with latent infections often present in asymptomatic tissues—especially young flush and fruit peduncles—treatment must extend beyond visibly symptomatic leaves. A full-canopy copper-based bactericide application is warranted at early disease detection to suppress inoculum buildup, protect emerging susceptible tissue, and reduce secondary spread, particularly before forecasted rainfall or pruning events.

Q1:
<image>
Why are the spots all clustered near the central vein of the leaf?
Q2: What causes the concentration of spots around the leaf's central vein?
label: Lesions are densely distributed along the main veins, reflecting the rapid systemic spread of the pathogen (Xanthomonas citri subsp. citri) via the leaf vascular system: after invasion, bacteria preferentially colonize water and nutrient transport pathways, causing lesions to develop linearly or in clusters along the midrib and lateral veins; this is not random distribution but visual evidence of systemic pathogen dissemination. Similar patterns are observed in other vascular-invading diseases, but the combination with raised, corky appearance still points specifically to citrus canker.

Q1:
<image>
If bugs like this are on stems but the plant looks fine, what damage might show up next?
Q2: What symptoms may develop next if these insects are present on the stems but no visible plant damage is currently apparent?
label: Although the current plant stems show no lesions or deformation, grasshopper nymphs feed by chewing—early damage appears as irregular notches or small holes along leaf margins or tender stems. Since this nymph is positioned on slender stems (likely young growth), monitor nearby leaves within 2–3 days for: (1) ragged edges on new leaves; (2) linear feeding scars on stems; (3) missing apical tissue if feeding intensifies. Check leaf undersides and newly emerged tillers, as nymphs often hide there during daylight. Absence of visible damage now suggests early infestation stage, before significant tissue loss occurs.

Q1:
<image>
This leaf has a yellow-green color with a dark brown spot near the center and uneven pigmentation—could it be citrus greening disease?
Q2: Does this leaf, showing yellow-green discoloration, a central dark brown spot, and irregular pigmentation, exhibit symptoms consistent with citrus greening disease?
label: Yes, this is highly consistent with Huanglongbing (HLB) in citrus: the non-symmetrical mottling (yellow-green patches not mirrored across the midrib), localized dark necrotic spots, and the absence of insect vectors or mechanical damage match the classic mottled yellowing phase. HLB-infected leaves often exhibit such asymmetric discoloration starting on individual branches; confirmation requires PCR testing of leaf tissue, but visual symptoms strongly suggest infection by Ca. Liberibacter asiaticus.

Q1:
<image>
If I see this on a few fruits like this one, what’s the first thing I should do before spraying?
Q2: What immediate action should be taken upon observing this symptom on a small number of fruits, prior to applying any spray?
label: First, inspect nearby leaves—especially older ones—for small black speckles on the underside, as leaf infection usually precedes fruit symptoms; if confirmed, prune and destroy all symptomatic leaves and fallen fruit to reduce inoculum; only then apply a protectant fungicide like 75% mancozeb (500×) to the entire canopy, focusing on new growth and fruit clusters, starting at early symptom detection to prevent further spread.

Q1:
<image>
This tiny clear bug with long hairs and a rounded body—could it be a spider mite?
Q2: Does the image show a small, translucent insect with elongated hairs and a globular shape, characteristic of a spider mite?
label: Yes, this is consistent with a twospotted spider mite (Tetranychus urticae) or closely related species in the Tetranychidae family. Key visual evidence includes its translucent oval body, fine setae (hair-like appendages) radiating from the perimeter, and internal segmentation visible through the cuticle—typical of adult or nymphal mites. The absence of dark spots suggests it may be unfed or a male; females often show two dark gut spots when fed. Without plant context or coloration, species-level ID is uncertain, but morphological features strongly support a spider mite.

Q1:
<image>
Can I spray just the affected fruit, or do I need to treat the whole tree?
Q2: Is it sufficient to apply treatment only to the symptomatic fruit, or must the entire tree be treated?
label: Spraying only the affected fruit is ineffective—spores are likely dispersed across the canopy. Treat the entire tree, especially new growth and leaf undersides, because: (1) invisible latent infections exist on asymptomatic tissue; (2) wind/rain will re-inoculate treated fruit from untreated zones; (3) Alternaria produces abundant secondary spores within days. Use a broad-spectrum protectant (e.g., 75% chlorothalonil 600×) with good coverage; repeat every 7 days for 2–3 applications if humidity persists. For organic systems, copper-lime sprays (e.g., Bordeaux) applied preventively are preferred, but avoid post-infection use on ripe fruit due to phytotoxicity risk.

Q1:
<image>
Can I use a natural spray on this caterpillar without hurting bees?
Q2: Is there a bee-safe natural spray that can be applied to the caterpillars visible in this image?
label: Yes—Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) is highly specific to caterpillars, non-toxic to bees, beneficial insects, and mammals, and approved for organic use; apply it directly to foliage where the larva is feeding, especially on new flush, in the evening to avoid UV degradation. Avoid broad-spectrum insecticides like pyrethroids, which harm pollinators and natural enemies such as Hyposoter wasps that commonly parasitize this pest.

Q1:
<image>
Can Bordeaux mixture be used? Is it safe to spray it directly onto the leaves?
Q2: Is it safe to apply Bordeaux mixture directly to the leaves?
label: Application is possible but should be done with caution: the image shows mature leaves rather than tender tissues, which generally exhibit better tolerance to copper-based formulations. It is recommended to use the 3-2-6-100 Bordeaux mixture (copper sulfate: lime: water = 3:2:100), diluted and evenly sprayed, focusing on both sides of the affected leaves and surrounding healthy foliage. Avoid application during high temperatures (>30°C) to prevent phytotoxicity; if tree vigor is weak or sulfur-containing pesticides were recently applied, conduct a small-scale test spray first. This approach is suitable for organic orchards.

Q1:
<image>
Why does this leaf have only one insect, yet several discolored spots around it?
Q2: What causes the multiple discolored spots surrounding the single insect on this leaf?
label: A single female red wax scale can cause multiple distal injuries: its stylets repeatedly pierce plant tissues, disrupting vascular pathways and triggering local nutrient deficiency and oxidative stress, which leads to necrotic spots even in regions not directly contacted. Additionally, metabolic byproducts (such as organic acids) from the insect may spread along leaf veins, exacerbating degeneration in adjacent tissues. Moreover, the insect has entered the pre-oviposition stage (the central reddish-brown dot marks the ovisac opening), and internal nutrient depletion further increases the physiological burden on the host plant. Note: if the spots expand over the next few days or new insects appear, it indicates population spread; however, if only one insect is present and the lesion remains stable, it likely represents an isolated, accidental invasion.

Q1:
<image>
If I find caterpillars like this one alone on a white background, what should I check on the tree right now?
Q2: What should be examined on the tree at this moment upon observing a solitary caterpillar like the one shown against a white background?
label: Check newly flushed terminals for rolled or tied leaves—especially on the outer canopy of south/east-facing branches. Even a single larva indicates active infestation; look for silk-bound leaf clusters where the larva feeds internally, leaving only the upper epidermis intact (translucent 'window' patches). Open any suspected rolls: if you find a live worm inside, count it as an infested terminal. At this stage, damage may be subtle but cumulative feeding can cause terminal curling or dieback within days.

Q1:
<image>
Can I just spray something now since the butterfly is here, even if I don’t see caterpillars?
Q2: Is it appropriate to apply a treatment at this stage, given the presence of the butterfly but no visible caterpillars?
label: No—spraying without confirmed larvae is ineffective and harmful. Adults are not controlled by foliar insecticides targeting caterpillars, and prophylactic spraying kills beneficial insects and risks resistance. Instead, use cultural control: remove nearby sweet fennel (a preferred alternate host) or plant it as a trap crop away from trees, then mow it after peak egg-laying. Only treat when live larvae ≥2 mm are observed on new growth.

Q1:
<image>
Is this a healthy leaf or one with disease? It’s grayish, has tiny black dots all over, and two deeper holes near the top.
Q2: Does this leaf show signs of disease, based on its grayish color, widespread tiny black dots, and two deeper holes near the top?
label: This is a diseased citrus leaf, specifically showing advanced citrus canker. Healthy citrus leaves are uniformly green (or yellow-green when senescing), smooth, and lack symmetrical crater-like depressions. The pervasive speckling and paired sunken pits indicate bacterial proliferation and tissue necrosis. The grayscale appearance in the image reflects loss of chlorophyll and lignification—consistent with canker’s progression to corky, dead tissue. No other common citrus leaf disease produces this combination of bilateral pustule collapse and diffuse speckling.

Q1:
<image>
The spots look dark and a bit sunken—what stage of disease does that suggest on this leaf?
Q2: What disease stage is indicated by the dark, slightly sunken spots visible on this leaf?
label: Dark, slightly sunken spots on the upper leaf surface indicate the intermediate to late phase of citrus canker development: after initial oil-soaked lesions, the tissue becomes necrotic and may develop a raised, corky margin as it matures. To confirm, flip the leaf and check the underside for corresponding raised, spongy pustules (early) or tan-to-brown, cratered lesions (mature). If the spots are dry and cracked, it suggests advanced木栓化 (corking), which often precedes leaf drop.

Q1:
<image>
What visual characteristics of the citrus fruit peels—specifically the morphology, distribution, and tissue-level changes associated with black spots—support a diagnosis of Citrus Black Spot (Guignardia citricarpa) rather than insect damage or mechanical injury?
Q2: What morphological features, spatial patterns, and tissue-level alterations are visible on the citrus fruit peels in the image that distinguish the black spots from insect damage or mechanical injury?
label: The diagnosis of Citrus Black Spot is supported by the presence of well-demarcated, subepidermal, melanized necrotic lesions on the flavedo layer—typically circular to irregular, 3–10 mm in diameter, with raised, dark brown to jet-black margins and often a chlorotic halo. These lesions lack epidermal rupture, frass, feeding punctures, or surrounding stippling, ruling out arthropod activity; they also show no linear abrasions, crushing deformities, or localized epidermal collapse indicative of mechanical injury. Critically, the lesions exhibit central stromatal development—visible as minute, embedded, black pycnidial structures under magnification—and maintain intact overlying cuticle, confirming fungal colonization rather than secondary invasion. The absence of associated mycelium on the surface and the exclusive localization to mature rind tissue further distinguish Citrus Black Spot from postharvest pathogens like Penicillium or Alternaria, which typically display conidial masses or water-soaked margins.

Q1:
<image>
What might cause these scattered brown spots without any bugs visible?
Q2: What could be responsible for the isolated brown lesions observed on the plant tissue, with no insects present?
label: The spots likely result from bacterial infection via wounds or natural openings, especially under wet conditions—rain splash or dew can carry Xanthomonas citri into stomata or micro-abrasions. Since no insects or mites are present, mechanical injury (e.g., wind abrasion, pruning cuts) or prolonged leaf wetness (>20 min) are probable entry routes. Multiple discrete lesions suggest repeated inoculation events rather than systemic spread.

Q1:
<image>
The leaves look as if they’ve been scalded, with scorched edges but green centers—could this be a sign of red spider mites?
Q2: Do the leaves show scorch-like damage along the edges while retaining green centers, suggesting red spider mite infestation?
label: Not spider mites. Typical symptoms of spider mite damage include dense, pale grayish-green stippling spots on the upper leaf surface, severe cases leading to complete whitening of the leaf and fine webbing covering the entire surface; on the underside, red/yellow specks (mite bodies) and silk webs can be observed. However, this image shows no webbing and no punctate chlorosis; instead, it exhibits extensive yellowing, marginal necrosis, and curling—consistent with tissue necrosis and growth abnormalities following aphid piercing-sucking feeding. Apple aphids are small in size, with a pale yellow to light green coloration, commonly hiding on the leaf undersides or inner surfaces of new shoots, making them difficult to detect without a magnifying lens.

Q1:
<image>
Based on visible morphological and behavioral features in the image—including black-and-yellow banding, fleshy osmeterium eversion, feeding damage characterized by semi-circular notches along leaf margins, and accumulation of greenish-brown frass pellets near petioles—can Bacillus thuringiensis var. kurstaki (Bt) still be effectively applied against the California citrus swallowtail larva, or has it likely progressed beyond the susceptible third-instar stage indicated by head capsule width exceeding 1.2 mm and absence of active leaf consumption?
Q2: Based on visible morphological and behavioral features in the image—including black-and-yellow banding, eversion of a fleshy osmeterium, semi-circular notches along leaf margins, and greenish-brown frass pellets near petioles—can Bacillus thuringiensis var. kurstaki (Bt) still be effectively applied, or has the larva likely advanced beyond the third-instar stage, as indicated by a head capsule width exceeding 1.2 mm and lack of active leaf feeding?
label: Bacillus thuringiensis var. kurstaki remains effective only against early-instar California citrus swallowtail larvae, typically up to the third instar, when midgut pH and receptor expression permit toxin binding and pore formation. Visual confirmation of efficacy windows requires assessing three key image-based cues: first, head capsule width relative to leaf venation—instars beyond 1.2 mm indicate fourth or fifth instar, where peritrophic membrane thickening and protease upregulation confer Bt resistance; second, feeding behavior—active notching of leaf margins with fresh green frass suggests ongoing consumption and potential susceptibility, whereas cessation of feeding, body elongation, and wandering behavior signal pre-pupal migration; third, integumental morphology—loss of distinct banding contrast, cuticular dullness, and reduced osmeterium responsiveness indicate developmental progression toward pupation. In this image, the larva exhibits taut, waxy cuticle, minimal frass deposition, and no visible osmeterium eversion during gentle disturbance, confirming late-instar status and rendering Bt application biologically ineffective.

Q1:
<image>
Why do some leaves show jagged holes near the tips while others look untouched—even though they’re on the same branch?
Q2: Why do certain leaves on the same branch exhibit irregular holes near their tips, while adjacent leaves remain intact?
label: This uneven damage reflects the feeding preference of adult gray weevils for tender, newly expanded foliage. Leaves with notches are likely younger, recently unfurled leaves that were accessible when adults emerged; older, tougher leaves remain intact. To verify, inspect leaf undersides and check for fresh feeding marks on new flushes—especially on terminal shoots—and compare damage severity between current-season vs. prior-season growth.

Q1:
<image>
The leaves are curled into tubes with ragged edges, and there are spider-web-like substances nearby—is this caused by red spider mites or another type of insect?
Q2: Are the leaf tubes with ragged edges and adjacent spider-web-like materials associated with red spider mites or a different insect?
label: Not spider mites: Spider mite damage typically manifests as dense, pale green stippling across the entire leaf surface, with rusty webbing on the leaf underside, and lacks distinct edge notches or leaf rolling. The observed symptoms—leaf rolling, irregular notching, and translucent fine silk threads—are more consistent with early-stage larval activity or adult feeding disturbance by gray longhorn beetle. Gray longhorn beetle larvae are milky white and legless; newly hatched larvae spin delicate silk threads at leaf margins to create slight rolls for shelter, while adults directly chew notches into leaves. The silk network is non-characteristic of typical spider webs (lacking radial patterns), and shows no signs of mite-specific molt casings or fecal pellets. Therefore, this damage is identified as being caused by gray longhorn beetles rather than mites (confidence = 0.85).

Q1:
<image>
The middle part of this leaf shows yellowing with uneven coloration near the main vein, but there are no black spots or mold layers—what could be causing this issue?
Q2: What is causing the irregular yellowing around the central vein of this leaf, with no black spots or fungal growth visible?
label: These are symptoms of silver-white mottling or chlorotic spots resulting from thrips feeding damage. Both adults and nymphs use a rasping-sucking mouthpart to scrape epidermal cells and suck sap, leading to localized death of mesophyll cells and degradation of chlorophyll, manifesting as irregular pale yellow to silvery patches that often cluster along the veins. Since no secondary fungal or bacterial infections are present, there are no distinct lesions, mold layers, or necrotic rings. Field verification method: Flip the leaves and examine the underside under a magnifier for tiny crawling insects or empty exuviae; if new shoots show more severe symptoms than older leaves, this supports ongoing thrips infestation.

Q1:

Why would the trunk spontaneously exude such a large amount of gum in areas that have neither been bitten by insects nor physically damaged?
Q2: What causes the trunk to produce excessive gum exudation in the absence of insect feeding or physical injury?
label: Spontaneous gummosis occurring without external trauma is primarily due to latent fungi (e.g., Neoscytalidium dimidiatum) invading through micro-wounds or stomata when tree vigor is compromised (e.g., under heat stress, water deficiency, or rapid shoot growth phases). The gum distribution observed in the image is near branch meristematic tissues—areas with thin bark and high metabolic activity, making them susceptible entry points. Additionally, background signs include slightly curled leaves and dry soil, suggesting recent heat stress or moisture deficit, which weakened the tree’s defensive capacity. Furthermore, if nearby branches are already infected, their powdery spores (the small dark spots visible in the image may represent early accumulations) can be dispersed via wind or splash, leading to secondary infections.

Q1:
<image>
This leaf has yellow-green mottling and a few dark spots—could it be citrus canker?
Q2: Does this leaf show yellow-green mottling and dark spots consistent with citrus canker?
label: Yes, the combination of diffuse chlorotic mottling (light green/yellow speckling) with discrete dark brown to black necrotic spots on the lamina is highly consistent with early-stage citrus canker caused by Xanthomonas citri subsp. citri. The absence of raised, corky margins or pustules suggests it is not yet in the advanced ulcerated phase, but the spot morphology and distribution match initial infection symptoms on leaves.

Q1:
<image>
Why would this mite be found alone instead of in groups on a leaf?
Q2: Why is this mite observed singly rather than in clusters on the leaf?
label: Citrus bud mites live concealed inside bud scales or fruit buttons—not exposed on leaf surfaces—so solitary individuals are typically collected during sampling; group outbreaks occur internally and become visible only after bud death or distortion, making early detection reliant on proactive bud inspection rather than leaf surveys.

Q1:
<image>
Why would black spots appear only on one side of the fruit, especially clustered on the upper right part?
Q2: What causes the black spots localized exclusively to the upper right portion of the fruit?
label: This asymmetric clustering suggests localized infection from external inoculum sources: rain-splashed spores from nearby infected fruit or leaves most commonly land on the upper-exposed surface; mechanical injury (e.g., branch rub) or cold damage on that quadrant creates entry points for *Septoria citri*, which preferentially infects weakened tissue. Additionally, the glossy sheen indicates recent moisture retention—dew or light rain—which promotes spore germination on that side. Multiple factors likely interact: microclimate (exposure), tissue vulnerability, and directional splash dispersal.

Q1:
<image>
Are these spots likely from rain splash or from bugs scratching the leaf?
Q2: Do the spots on the leaf appear to be caused by rain splash or by insect damage?
label: Both are plausible, but rain splash is more probable here: the spots are distributed across the lamina and near veins—not concentrated at petiole junctions or along edges where wind/abrasion injuries typically occur. Bacterial canker requires a water film for entry, and the uniform green background suggests no recent mechanical trauma (e.g., thorn punctures or insect feeding scars). However, if the tree is in a windy orchard with thorny varieties, minor abrasions could serve as secondary entry points; thus, multiple factors may contribute.

Q1:
<image>
There are dozens of them clumped on one leaf—should I spray right away?
Q2: Are there dozens of these clustered on a single leaf, warranting immediate treatment?
label: Not yet—on mature trees, aphid colonies under 40% of new flushes infested rarely require treatment, as natural enemies (lady beetles, lacewings, parasitoid wasps) usually suppress them within 6 weeks; instead, monitor daily for predators or mummies (swollen, tan aphid cadavers indicating parasitism). If leaf curling worsens or honeydew becomes sticky, apply narrow-range oil (0.5%) only to affected shoots—not whole tree—to preserve beneficials.

Q1:
<image>
The leaves are curled and have irregular holes, but despite taking photos for a long time, no insects have been found—where could they be hiding?
Q2: What is causing the leaf curling and irregular holes in the absence of visible insects?
label: Adult gray weevils are nocturnal, hiding during the day in bark crevices, under leaf litter, or near the roots of nearby weeds; larvae inhabit the soil surface or the base of tender shoots, not attaching to leaf surfaces. Eggs are laid in the narrow gap between the margins of the top two mature leaves on twigs, where they are difficult to detect visually. Thus, "symptoms without visible insects" is the norm. It is recommended to collect adults in the early morning or late afternoon using the white cloth-shaking method, or to examine the base of damaged leaves for pale white, legless larvae—whose cryptic behavior results in no visible insect body in images, yet symptoms clearly point to this pest.

Q1:
<image>
Is this the same pest that leaves white zigzag trails on citrus fruit?
Q2: Does this image show the pest responsible for white zigzag trails on citrus fruit?
label: Yes. The brown garden snail produces characteristic bright white, glossy mucus trails—especially visible on smooth surfaces like fruit rinds or leaves—as seen by the wet sheen on its body and the dew-covered leaf. Those trails dry into persistent silvery lines, often accompanied by black fecal spots near feeding sites.

Q1:
<image>
I spotted this butterfly today—what’s the best first step before spraying?
Q2: What is the appropriate initial action to take upon observing this butterfly?
label: First, scout 20–30 young terminals for eggs or small caterpillars; if fewer than 1–2 larvae per shoot, use hand-removal or prune infested tips. If larvae are present and feeding, apply Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) to new growth only—spray in late afternoon during warm, dry weather for best efficacy. Avoid broad-spectrum insecticides to protect parasitic wasps like Hyposoter sp., which naturally suppress populations.

Q1:
<image>
The number of small red spots on the fruit is increasing, yet the leaves remain healthy. What could be happening?
Q2: Why are small red spots multiplying on the fruit while the leaves show no signs of damage?
label: This represents a typical early manifestation of citrus rust mite infestation: mites preferentially feed on young fruit epidermis before symptoms appear on leaves. Mites congregate on the fruit surface—especially on shaded sides and in the depression around the calyx—where they suck sap from oil gland cells, causing localized tissue necrosis and forming small red-brown to rusty spots. Due to their minute size and cryptic behavior, live mites are invisible to the naked eye, leaving leaf surfaces smooth and intact. Immediate inspection is advised by flipping the fruit to examine the pedicel base and surrounding calyx area—if dense spots and slightly dull skin are observed, it confirms active mite infestation. If left unchecked, the fruit surface will turn coppery or black-brown within 2–3 weeks (“burnt orange”), resulting in significant loss of market value.

Q1:

Is this round, orange-yellow with spiral patterns in the center and a white outer edge actually the female adult shell of the red wax scale insect?

label: This is the waxy test of a mature female red wax scale (Ceroplastes rubens). The image clearly shows typical characteristics: a central orange-brown elevation with concentric rings and spiral patterns, surrounded by a white waxy margin, forming a circular, convex structure firmly attached to the plant surface—these are hallmark morphological features of mature female tests in C. rubens. In contrast, the brown soft scale (Coccus hesperidum) has a flatter test without distinct spiral patterns and a thinner, semi-transparent wax layer, thus ruling it out. The identification is based on clear visualization of wax structural details and color stratification, with high confidence.

Q2: Does this orange exhibit dark spots scattered across its peel?
label: Yes, the scattered irregular dark spots on the yellow-orange peel, especially when concentrated near the calyx and lacking sunken margins or fruiting bodies, are consistent with early-stage Alternaria black spot (caused by Alternaria alternata). Septoria spot typically shows more defined sunken lesions with black fruiting bodies in advanced stages, which are not visible here. The absence of deep pitting or albedo involvement further supports black spot over Septoria.

Q1:
<image>
The fruit looks shiny overall, but the black spots don’t reflect light—what does that texture difference mean?
Q2: Why do the black spots on the fruit appear non-reflective compared to the surrounding shiny surface?
label: The glossy sheen indicates intact cuticle and oil glands on healthy rind, while the non-reflective black spots suggest loss of epicuticular wax and cell collapse due to fungal necrosis. In black spot disease, the pathogen degrades host tissue, causing localized death and pigment accumulation (melanin in Alternaria), which absorbs light instead of reflecting it. This textural contrast is a reliable field indicator of active infection versus superficial soiling or dust. To verify, gently rub a spot—if it smudges black, it’s likely fungal; if it wipes off cleanly, it may be dirt or sap exudate.

Q1:
<image>
The leaf surface has black spots and feels slightly sticky—could this be caused by honeydew excreted by insects?
Q2: Are the black spots on the leaf surface accompanied by a sticky residue indicative of insect-produced honeydew?
label: It is highly likely that the sooty mold observed was induced by honeydew secreted after feeding by brown soft scales. The black spots on the leaf surface appear dry and brittle in texture, yet some areas exhibit slight sheen and moisture, consistent with early-stage honeydew crystallization before fungal colonization. During feeding, both nymphs and adults extract phloem sap and excrete excess sugars as honeydew, which attracts sooty mold fungi (e.g., Capnodium spp.), leading to loosely adherent black fungal layers. Note: if the black spots can be scraped off as powder, this indicates typical sooty mold; if they remain glossy and sticky, they represent fresh honeydew. These two often coexist, forming a characteristic triad of “insect–honeydew–fungus.”

Q1:

Could these spots be Septoria spot instead of black spot, since they’re on a ripe orange?
Q2: Are these spots on the ripe orange consistent with Septoria spot rather than black spot?
label: Unlikely. Septoria spot typically shows *sunken*, sharply defined pits that extend into the white albedo, often with visible black fruiting bodies embedded in the lesion—and symptoms intensify *after* harvest during storage. Here, the spots are superficial, non-pitted, and lack embedded structures; the larger lesion near the stem is diffuse rather than crater-like. Also, Septoria rarely causes such concentrated stem-end lesions. Visual evidence favors Alternaria black spot.

Q2: Why are insects observed resting on the slender green leaves instead of on thicker branches or older foliage?
label: This pest prefers feeding on tender tissues because young needle-like leaves have high moisture content, elevated amino acid concentration, and low mechanical resistance, all of which facilitate penetration by its piercing-sucking mouthparts. In the image, the insect is tightly pressed against the needle surface with its front legs slightly flexed in a grasping posture, indicating it is positioning itself for feeding; mature leaves have thick epidermis and strong cuticular wax layers that are difficult to penetrate. Additionally, the clustered structure of needle foliage provides concealment, reducing the likelihood of detection by natural enemies. This behavior reflects a coordinated adaptation to both nutritional needs and predator avoidance strategies.

label: Not newly hatched. Newly hatched nymphs are wingless, pale in color (typically light green or milky white), and have short antennae; the individual in the image possesses fully developed transparent wings, distinct abdominal bands, and dark brown body coloration, indicating a mature winged adult that has undergone multiple molts and is capable of long-distance flight; such individuals typically appear during the vigorous growth phase of new shoots in spring, originating from successive generations produced by overwintering eggs, marking a critical stage in population expansion.

Q1:
<image>
A citrus leaf exhibits bilateral asymmetry in discoloration—approximately half the lamina is green while the other half shows yellow-brown chlorosis and necrosis, with upward curling and marginal scorch-like desiccation; what pest causes this specific pattern of injury, and how do these visual features collectively support that diagnosis?
Q2: What pest is responsible for the bilateral asymmetry in discoloration on this citrus leaf—where one half remains green and the other half displays yellow-brown chlorosis, necrosis, upward curling, and marginal scorch-like desiccation?
label: This symptom complex is caused by the citrus leaf beetle (Gonioctena aenescens), whose feeding behavior induces asymmetric foliar damage through highly localized, repeated epidermal puncturing and mesophyll sap extraction along one side of the midrib. The resulting bilateral mottling arises not from systemic infection but from unilateral phytotoxic saliva injection and vascular disruption, leading to progressive interveinal chlorosis on the affected side, followed by necrotic browning due to oxidative stress and secondary epidermal collapse. Marginal upward curling occurs as a turgor response to asymmetric cell wall degradation and loss of structural integrity in the damaged tissue, while the scorched appearance reflects advanced desiccation and cuticular rupture at the leaf edge—distinct from fungal or nutritional etiologies due to the sharp demarcation, absence of sporulation or vein banding, and consistent association with adult beetle presence and characteristic shallow, irregular notching confined to the discolored margin.

label: Yes—it effectively rules out both. Fungal leaf spots show discrete lesions, necrotic centers, or concentric rings; mite damage causes stippling, bronzing, or fine webbing—none of which appear here. This leaf has uniform color transition, intact edges, and no surface texture changes, aligning with physiological disruption from HLB rather than direct tissue destruction. Still, lab confirmation is essential because nutrient deficiencies (e.g., Zn, Fe) can mimic this pattern.

Q2: Are the small, raised, semi-transparent bumps on the leaf—about the size of rice grains and showing faint yellow spots—red wax scale insects?
label: These are female adults or nymphs of *Ceroplastes floridensis*. Evidence: the organisms appear as circular to irregularly shaped, convex elevations with a thin, semi-transparent wax layer on the surface, often featuring a pale yellow to light brown spot at the center (likely the site of mouthpart penetration or internal contents), densely distributed across the leaf surface without any webbing structure—characteristic of the typical morphology of *C. floridensis* females feeding in fixed positions. This differs from mealybugs (which possess white wax filaments) and armored scales (with hard, sharply defined shells), confirming that the observed features closely match those of *C. floridensis*.

Q2: Do the varying sizes of leaf gaps and notches in the image indicate feeding by distinct insect species?
label: Variations in notch size reflect differences in feeding intensity and duration: large notches are typically due to sustained feeding by adult beetles (e.g., adult gray snout beetles can consume over one-third of a leaf margin in a single feeding event), while small notches may result from initial exploratory feeding by newly hatched larvae or brief visits by adult insects. Different developmental stages of the same species can produce a gradient of damage—gray snout beetle larvae are pale white and legless, living in soil and not directly feeding on leaves, so any leaf surface notches must be caused by adults. It is recommended to assess the damage level based on the number of notches on new shoots and whether they are concentrated on shoots during the greening phase: 2–3 notches per plant with damage constitutes level 1; 4–6 notches constitute level 2, requiring graded response measures. confidence: 0.89

Q2: Does this yellow-orange fruit with scattered small black spots on its skin show signs of black spot disease?
label: Yes, the scattered dark brown to black spots on a mature citrus fruit surface are consistent with Alternaria black spot (caused by Alternaria alternata), especially when spots are discrete, irregular, and lack sunken margins or fruiting bodies. However, Septoria spot also causes similar black spots on ripe fruit; definitive diagnosis requires checking for sunken lesions or black pycnidia under magnification. Given the non-sunken, glossy-surface appearance here, black spot is more likely than Septoria spot, which typically shows deeper pits and albedo involvement.

Q2: Is this insect on the ground because it has recently emerged from the soil?
label: Yes, this insect likely has just completed pupal eclosion and emerged from the soil. The citrus fruit fly overwinters as pupae in the soil layer 3–10 cm below the surface. In spring, when temperature and humidity are favorable, adults emerge and must push through the soil layer to reach the surface. Initially, they rest on exposed ground or low-lying rocks until their exoskeleton hardens and wings fully expand before flying toward the canopy. The image shows the insect lying flat without flight posture, with a uniform gravelly soil background—characteristics fully consistent with those of newly emerged adults in their typical behavior and microhabitat.

Q1:

Q2: Is it appropriate to apply an organic spray at this stage, or should application be delayed until further damage is visible?
label: Yes, apply organic Bt *now* if the tree is young and the caterpillar is feeding—delaying until visible damage risks losing critical leaf area needed for establishment. Bt works best on small-to-medium larvae, and this specimen appears mature (full banding, robust size), so timing is urgent. Spray thoroughly on all foliage, focusing on new growth where feeding concentrates; reapply after rain or in 5–7 days if new larvae appear. Do not wait for holes or defoliation—early intervention prevents yield loss.

Q1:

Does this leaf belong to a sick citrus tree, and if so, what’s the most probable disease?
Q2: Is the citrus leaf in the image showing signs of disease, and if yes, what disease is most likely indicated?
label: Yes, this leaf strongly suggests Huanglongbing (HLB) in citrus. Key visual evidence includes: (1) non-symmetrical yellow-green mottling across the lamina, (2) preserved dark green along midrib and lateral veins, (3) slight puckering without holes, tears, or insect presence, and (4) entire, undamaged margins. These features distinguish HLB from citrus greening mimics like citrus tristeza virus (which causes vein corking and stem pitting) or nutrient disorders (which lack asymmetry). Final confirmation requires molecular testing, but visually, HLB is the most probable diagnosis.

label: Possibly, but not definitively—the moth is the adult stage, while damage is caused by larvae. If the damage includes serpentine mines, leaf rolling, or frass-filled folds on new growth, and the moth was collected nearby within 1–2 weeks of symptom onset, causality is likely. Confirm by checking for live larvae inside damaged leaves or pupal cases in rolled edges; absence of larvae suggests another pest (e.g., citrus leafminer) may be responsible.

label: It is not caused by chewing damage but by piercing-sucking feeding. Lepidosaphes beckii uses its stylets to penetrate mesophyll tissue or bark to feed on sap, leading to localized necrosis and chlorosis, resulting in yellow spots or ring-shaped chlorotic zones. In severe cases, marginal leaf tissues dry out and fragment into irregular holes (distinct from chewed-out lesions). Check the underside of damaged leaves—if dense scale insects are found corresponding to yellow patches on the upper surface, it confirms piercing-sucking injury. Additional typical symptoms include yellowing and curling of new leaves, and premature dropping of older leaves.

Q1:

Q2: Does the image show a small, reddish-brown, segmented, and shiny insect bearing black spots that is a locust nymph?
label: This is a locust nymph. Evidence: the reddish-brown coloration with dark spots, smooth and glossy body surface, clearly segmented structure, absence of fully developed wings (only small wing buds are visible), and robust hind legs (part of the femur profile is visible in the lower right corner of the image) all conform to typical characteristics of nymphs in the superfamily Acridoidea (Orthoptera). In contrast to nymphs of crickets or bush crickets, this specimen has short antennae (although not fully visible in the image, head proportions support the inference of short antennae) and lacks long filamentous appendages. This morphology is commonly observed in second- to third-instar nymph stages.

Q1:

label: This represents typical early symptoms of citrus canker. Multiple irregularly shaped, slightly raised lesions—deep brown to black—are clustered on the upper part of the leaf surface, exhibiting a waxy sheen (indicating dried bacterial exudate). The leaf margins remain intact without perforations or tearing—consistent with initial stages of citrus canker (2–10 mm greasy spots → raised pustules → suberized necrosis). This differs from fungal spot diseases (typically sunken and powdery) or bacterial wilting (darkened petiole bases and entire leaf drooping). According to the knowledge base, after infection by Xanthomonas citri subsp. citri, lesions commonly develop into spongy elevations that eventually become corky, matching the image closely.

Insect eggs are typically oval, translucent or surrounded by a gelatinous sheath, and are usually laid on the abaxial surface of leaves or on tender shoots. It is recommended to examine the leaf underside for possible presence of psyllid nymphs or honeydew residues—if the abaxial surface is clean, free of insects and honeydew, this further supports a pathological origin of the necrotic spots.

label: This is a citrus leafminer, not a peelminer. Leafminers have slender bodies, silvery-white forewings with faint striations and a dark apical spot, and fringed hindwings—exactly as shown. Peelminers are slightly larger, lack the prominent abdominal tuft, and their pupal cocoons have decorative silk balls (not visible here, but consistent with absence of such structures in this image). The absence of fruit/stem damage context further supports leafminer identification.

Q1:

This leaf is already damaged; is it still effective to apply pesticide now? And where exactly should it be sprayed?
Q2: Given the visible damage on this leaf, is pesticide application still effective at this stage, and what specific areas require spraying?
label: The affected leaf already shows moderate to severe symptoms, so chemical control has limited efficacy on this individual leaf, but can prevent disease spread to adjacent healthy leaves: immediately apply a systemic fungicide (e.g., dimethomorph or metalaxyl) to the entire plant, focusing especially on the underside of middle-to-lower leaves and the base of the main veins—because Phytophthora spores readily germinate on the leaf undersides, and the pathogen spreads upward via vascular bundles. Simultaneously, remove and deeply bury or incinerate the infected leaf to avoid it becoming a secondary inoculum source. If overall orchard humidity is high, also clear drainage ditches and prune overly dense branches to reduce leaf wetness duration. Never treat only the diseased leaf—protective treatment of the entire plant is essential.

Q1:

label: This is the testaceous shell of the female adult of Aonidiella aurantii. Evidence includes: ① Shape is nearly circular, roughly the size of a fingernail tip; ② Shell base color ranges from orange-yellow to orange-red, with a dark concentric ring pattern at the center (appearing as dense black dots in the image—these are actually the "umbilicus" and pigment deposits at the center of mature female shells); ③ Surface is smooth and glossy, consistent with hardened waxy shell characteristics; ④ No plant tissue adheres to the shell, confirming its detached state after collection. This morphology closely matches the typical female shell of California red scale, effectively ruling out yellow scale (which has lighter yellow shells, sparser central dark spots, and is more commonly found on fruits rather than branches and leaves).

label: The textured surface with small raised dots on the fruit is typical of citrus peel morphology (oil glands), not direct pest injury; however, the proximity of heavily notched leaves to the fruit indicates high risk of egg-laying on the fruit button later. Gray weevil adults feed on leaves but lay eggs primarily under the fruit button or in bark crevices—not on the peel itself. So while the fruit isn’t currently damaged, its location among damaged foliage signals imminent oviposition threat, especially if adults emerge soon.

Q1:

The flower where the butterfly is resting in the image is not a citrus flower, and the adjacent citrus leaves appear healthy—what control measures should be taken at this stage to prevent a caterpillar outbreak?
Q2: Given that the flower with the butterfly is non-citrus and nearby citrus leaves show no symptoms, what preventive actions are appropriate now to avoid caterpillar infestation?
label: Preventive cultural and biological control measures should be implemented: since adults have already been observed on nearby nectar sources, oviposition is imminent. Immediately prune and remove alternative host plants such as sweet fennel along the orchard perimeter to reduce oviposition attraction. Simultaneously, release or protect natural enemies—such as ichneumonid wasps (Hyposoter sp.), which exhibit high parasitization rates on larvae. If isolated eggs are detected, apply Bt formulations locally to affected shoots to avoid nonspecific pesticides that could harm beneficial insects. Chemical control should only be considered when larvae reach the second instar or above and densities exceed 10 individuals per tree.

Evidence: Most insects in the image are newly hatched or low-instar nymphs, firmly attached but not yet secreting significant amounts of honeydew; the white specks may be molting remnants or wax secretions, not sooty mold (which appears as fluffy, continuous, gray-black patches). Q1:

Is this citrus blast or canker? The leaves have dark spots and curl a bit, but no obvious stem dieback.
Q2: Does this citrus plant show signs of blast or canker, based on dark leaf spots and mild leaf curling without stem dieback?
label: This is more consistent with citrus canker than blast. Citrus blast (Pseudomonas syringae) typically starts at the petiole, causing girdling, rapid wilting, and twig dieback—none observed here. The scattered dark spots on lamina with marginal yellowing and mild curling match early canker symptoms. Blast lesions are usually smaller, blacker, and concentrated near leaf bases; canker lesions are larger (2–10 mm), irregular, and often surrounded by yellow halos. Without petiole necrosis or twig death, canker is the higher-probability diagnosis.

Q2: Do the small black dots arranged in rows on the insect's body represent eggs or natural markings?
label: The regularly spaced small black dots along the sides of the larva in the image are thoracic spiracles or pigment spots, not eggs. The citrus fruit fly larva lacks egg attachments on its body; eggs are pale white and oval-shaped, laid beneath the fruit skin and invisible externally. This feature helps distinguish it from certain Lepidopteran larvae (e.g., cutworms) that may exhibit mimicry patterns.

Q1:

Are the dark brown spots on these yellow fruits in the photo left by insects? They look like they've been bitten by small pests.
Q2: Do the dark brown spots on the yellow fruits in the image result from insect feeding damage?
label: This is not mechanical injury caused by insect bites, but rather necrotic spots on the fruit peel induced by feeding of Panonychus citri. The mite uses its stylet to pierce and suck sap from epidermal cells, triggering localized oxidative browning and forming irregular, poorly defined dark brown to black spots. In the image, these spots are concentrated on the lower to middle portion of the fruit, appearing scattered or fused—consistent with the mite’s preference for feeding during late fruit development stages. Although live mites are not visible, the spot morphology matches the typical progression of mite damage: initial silver-gray stippling progressing to browning. Thus, a preliminary diagnosis of damage by Panonychus citri is warranted.

Q1:

Why do the dark spots on this fruit look raised and uneven, and what does that mean for the tree?
Q2: What causes the raised, irregular dark spots visible on this fruit?
label: The raised, granular dark spots indicate localized necrosis and corky tissue formation caused by *Candidatus* Liberibacter asiaticus disrupting phloem function and triggering host defense responses. As the bacterium multiplies in sieve tubes, it blocks nutrient transport, leading to cell death, oxidation of phenolic compounds (causing browning), and secondary colonization by saprophytic fungi (e.g., *Alternaria* spp.), which can produce raised, textured lesions. This symptom typically appears in mid-to-late infection stages and correlates with poor fruit quality (dry, acidic, misshapen) and declining tree vigor. To verify, cut the fruit longitudinally: brown vascular tissue near the peduncle and aborted seeds confirm HLB. Also inspect nearby leaves for non-symmetrical mottling—especially on new flushes.

Q1:

Upon discovering such yellowed leaves, should we immediately apply pesticides, or should we first consider removing the tree?
Q2: Given the presence of yellowed leaves in the image, is pesticide application warranted immediately, or should tree removal be considered first?
label: Sampling and laboratory testing (PCR) should be prioritized—do not immediately cut down trees based on a single symptomatic leaf. If confirmed as HLB and the tree is in early stage (only a few branches show symptoms), the entire plant must be uprooted and destroyed. While awaiting results, apply imidacloprid or thiamethoxam to all plants within a 5-meter radius to control psyllids (focus on new shoots and abaxial leaf surfaces) to interrupt transmission. Avoid applying antibiotics solely to symptomatic leaves—trunk injection of tetracycline can only suppress bacteria temporarily, cannot cure the disease, and may promote resistance development; confidence: 0.85

Q1:

The middle of the leaf is yellow with green edges and slightly brownish dry margins—how severe is this? How can we determine if it's just an early-stage infection?
Q2: What is the severity of the leaf discoloration characterized by a yellow center, green margins, and slightly brown, dry edges—and how can early-stage progression be assessed from this image?
label: This represents the characteristic asymmetric mosaic yellowing typical of citrus greening disease, falling within the early to intermediate stage. To assess whether it is an initial outbreak, compare the affected leaf with older and younger leaves on the same branch: if the new growth also shows similar yellow-green mosaics, with no obvious nutrient deficiency rings at the petiole base (such as the inverse-V yellowing seen in zinc deficiency), and no signs of insect or chemical damage, the condition is more likely early-stage citrus greening. It is recommended to collect this leaf and the two adjacent new leaves for PCR testing, while simultaneously checking the branch for “red nose fruit” or small, deformed fruits as additional supporting evidence.

Q1:

Q2: What insect is depicted with large pincers and a reddish-brown body, and are the small yellow insects adjacent to it its offspring?
label: This is an adult European earwig (Forficula auricularia), characterized by reddish-brown body coloration, a reddish head, and prominent forceps-like cerci (pincer-like tail appendages) at the abdomen tip. The numerous small, pale yellowish-brown individuals surrounding it are nymphs, approximately one-third to one-half the size of adults, wingless, with clearly segmented bodies, visible antennae and legs—consistent with post-hatching aggregation behavior near the mother. The co-occurrence of adults and dense populations of nymphs concentrated among ground debris strongly supports this identification.

Q1:

The fruit appears to be covered with a layer of dark gray film, while the leaves remain green—is this condition severe?
Q2: Does the dark gray film on the fruit, with green leaves still present, indicate a serious condition?
label: This is a classic "rusty fruit" symptom caused by Panonychus citri: continuous feeding leads to death of epidermal cells and rupture of the cuticle, with accumulation of molted exoskeletons and oxidized compounds forming a gray-black membranous layer. If only one fruit shows localized symptoms, it indicates early, mild infestation; however, if dense silver-white speckles appear on the upper leaf surfaces (confirmed by checking the leaf undersides for mite colonies), it suggests population spread and possible progression into moderate damage—characterized by reduced photosynthetic efficiency, imbalanced sugar-acid ratio in fruits, increased risk of premature dropping, and post-harvest rot during storage. It is recommended to immediately inspect the undersides of five newly emerged leaves under a 10× magnifier for tiny red dots (adult mites) or translucent eggs.

Q1:
<image>
The leaf is already in this condition—would spraying fungicide still be effective? What treatment should be applied?
Q2: Given the current state of the leaf in the image, is fungicide application still effective, and what treatment is appropriate?
label: At this stage, the leaf is already severely infected; therefore, spraying primarily aims to prevent further spread of the pathogen to healthy tissues rather than curing the affected leaf. It is recommended to immediately remove and destroy infected leaves to reduce overwintering inoculum sources. Apply a protective spray of 50% carbendazim diluted 800-fold or 70% thiophanate-methyl diluted 1,000-fold to the entire tree, ensuring thorough coverage of the leaf undersides—since initial infection sites are predominantly located there. Repeat the treatment every 10–14 days for two applications. Meanwhile, enhance fertilization and irrigation to strengthen tree vigor and interrupt subsequent infection cycles.

Q2: Are the leaf margins showing yellowing and irregular black spots indicative of a disease?
label: Mild yellowing along leaf margins accompanied by localized black mold layers are typical symptoms of nutritional imbalance and impaired photosynthesis due to continuous feeding by brown soft scale. The black portions represent fungal mats formed by sooty mold growing on honeydew, not primary pathogens. It is recommended to examine the leaf undersides—if flat, oval-shaped, waxy, thin-shelled insects are found (especially distributed along main veins), the condition can be definitively diagnosed as secondary symptoms induced by scale insect infestation.

Q1:

Q2: Do the dark substances visible on the stems indicate that the fruits will later exhibit black discoloration of the skin?
label: Highly likely. The current concentration of damage on new shoots suggests the mite population has already established itself. Starting in mid-June, large numbers will migrate to young fruit surfaces to feed, disrupting oil glands and causing the fruit skin to lose luster, turning copper-black or bronze-colored (commonly known as "black-skinned fruit" or "burnt mandarin"). Even if the foliage currently shows no damage, as long as the mite source remains untreated, fruit will face extremely high risk of injury during the hot months of July–August. It is recommended to complete the first treatment before fruit diameter reaches 1.3 cm, and regularly inspect the stylar ends (base of the stigma) of inner fruits for silver-gray spotting.
